docs.title: Constitution of the Artifact-Driven Agent Runtime
docs.text:
Status: Foundational design document, aligned with reactifact 0.25.1 Version: 0.3 Purpose: Define the architectural philosophy, invariants, terminology, design rules, examples, and decision criteria for a new agent framework based on evolving typed artifacts and context rather than explicit execution graphs.

Terminology: this document uses agent for the conceptual state transformer. In the public API the container is StepGroup (a group of Steps that share triggers/retry/timeout); the old Agent name and the agents= keyword were removed in 0.24.

docs.title: 0. Executive Summary
docs.text:
This project is an agent runtime built around one central idea:

An agent does not primarily execute a workflow. An agent observes and transforms an evolving Context containing typed Artifacts.

The framework is intentionally different from graph-first agent frameworks.

Instead of asking developers to describe:

A → B → C → D

we ask them to describe:

What data exists?
What kinds of artifacts exist?
What can an agent do with those artifacts?
What conditions make an artifact useful, invalid, incomplete, or ready?

The runtime then coordinates execution around state changes.

The fundamental execution model is:

                  ┌──────────────────┐
                  │     Context      │
                  │                  │
                  │ Artifacts        │
                  │ References       │
                  │ Claims           │
                  │ Tasks            │
                  │ Events           │
                  └────────┬─────────┘
                           │
                           │ observed
                           ▼
                    ┌─────────────┐
                    │    Agent    │
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │
                           │ produces
                           ▼
                    ┌─────────────┐
                    │    Patch    │
                    └──────┬──────┘
                           │
                           │ applied
                           ▼
                  ┌──────────────────┐
                  │   Context v+1    │
                  └──────────────────┘
                           │
                           └───────↺

The core primitives are:

Context
Artifact
Reference
Agent
Patch
Event
Runtime
Source
Capability

The framework may internally use graphs, queues, DAGs, state machines, schedulers, vector indexes, databases, or LLM planners.

Those are implementation mechanisms.

They are not the primary programming model.

docs.title: 1.1 The problem
docs.text:
Modern agent frameworks commonly expose abstractions such as:

Chain
Graph
Node
Tool
Agent
Message
Memory
Workflow

These abstractions are useful, but complex applications often become difficult to express when the problem is not naturally a fixed workflow.

Knowledge-oriented agents are especially problematic.

A user can ask:

Why did infrastructure costs increase in Q2?

The answer may require:

  • Confluence documentation
  • GitLab Markdown
  • GitLab merge requests
  • GitLab commits
  • CSV files
  • XLS/XLSX spreadsheets
  • local Markdown
  • public landing pages
  • direct API calls
  • calculations
  • source verification
  • contradictory evidence
  • follow-up questions

There is no universal fixed graph.

One question may require:

Confluence → GitLab → CSV → answer

Another:

GitLab → GitLab → verification → answer

Another:

XLS → calculation → Confluence → GitLab → verification

Another may need only one source.

The framework therefore should not make the developer encode the exact execution path.

docs.title: 2.1 Agent as a state transformer
docs.text:
The canonical model is:

Agent(Context) → Effects      # effects.create/update/delete/link/upsert
                   │
                   ▼  runtime compiles (§24)
               Patch (atomic) → Context v+1

not:

Agent(Input) → Output

and not:

Node → Node

An agent reads a relevant view of the current Context and proposes changes.

Example:

class Researcher(Step):
    consumes = (Task,)
    produces = (Evidence,)

    async def run(self, task: Artifact[Task], effects: Effects) -> None:
        effects.create(Evidence(...))
        effects.update(task, status="researching")
        # nothing applied until the runtime compiles the effects

The step describes what should change (effects); the runtime compiles the effect set into one atomic Patch:

Context v12
   │
   │ Researcher (effects)
   ▼
Effects ──compile──▶ Patch ──apply──▶ Context v13

This distinction is foundational.

docs.title: 3. Why Context Exists
docs.text:
A Context is the current working state of a reasoning process.

It is not merely:

dict

It is not merely:

messages

It is not merely:

prompt_context

It represents the evolving state of a task.

Conceptually:

Context
├── Task
├── Questions
├── References
├── Artifacts
├── Evidence
├── Claims
├── Hypotheses
├── Calculations
├── Decisions
├── Events
└── Answers

A Context can evolve:

Context v1
   ↓
question added
   ↓
Context v2
   ↓
references discovered
   ↓
Context v3
   ↓
documents materialized
   ↓
Context v4
   ↓
claims extracted
   ↓
Context v5
   ↓
claims verified
   ↓
Context v6

The history is part of the system's observability.

docs.title: 4.1 Definition
docs.text:
An Artifact is a typed object representing something meaningful to the task.

Examples:

Question
Task
Document
ConfluencePage
GitLabFile
GitLabMergeRequest
GitLabCommit
Spreadsheet
SpreadsheetRange
MarkdownDocument
WebPage
Evidence
Claim
Hypothesis
Finding
Calculation
Report
Answer

Artifacts are first-class objects. A handle is an immutable typed snapshot; every revision lives in the Context's content-addressed ArtifactStore.

docs.title: 4.2 Artifact is not necessarily text
docs.text:
This is critical.

A spreadsheet should not automatically become:

"CSV converted to text"

A GitLab merge request should not automatically become:

"chunk of text"

A Confluence page should not automatically become:

"embedding"

Instead:

GitLabRepository
├── File
├── Commit
├── MergeRequest
├── Issue
└── Discussion

Workbook
├── Sheet
│   ├── Columns
│   └── Rows
└── NamedRanges

ConfluenceSpace
└── Page
    ├── Section
    ├── Table
    └── Link

Structure is preserved whenever practical. Falling back to flattened text is acceptable only as a stopgap before a proper typed Artifact exists for a source — it must not become the permanent representation for a domain the framework already models structurally (GitLab, Confluence, Spreadsheets).

docs.title: 5. Reference vs Artifact
docs.text:
This distinction is fundamental.

A Reference identifies something in an external system.

An Artifact is a materialized representation available for reasoning.

Example:

ConfluencePageRef
        │
        │ resolve()
        ▼
ConfluencePage

A reference may contain:

ConfluencePageRef(
    space="ENGINEERING",
    page_id="12345",
    title="Authentication Architecture",
)

It does not need to contain the entire page.

The page can be fetched later.

This makes References cheap and lazy.

docs.title: 6. Lazy Artifacts
docs.text:
External knowledge should not be eagerly loaded.

Example:

page = ConfluencePageRef(
    page_id="12345"
)

At this point:

metadata = available
content = not materialized

When needed:

page.resolve()

the connector accesses Confluence.

Conceptually:

Reference
├── locator
├── metadata
└── resolver
       │
       ▼
   external system
       │
       ▼
   Artifact

This is important because not every source is indexed or embedded.

docs.title: 7. Source
docs.text:
A Source describes an external system from which References or Artifacts can be obtained.

Examples:

GitLab
Confluence
Filesystem
Website
Database
S3
REST API

A Source is not an Agent.

A Source answers:

How can information be located or materialized?

An Agent answers:

What should be reasoned about or changed?

Example:

gitlab = GitLabSource(...)
confluence = ConfluenceSource(...)
filesystem = FileSystemSource(...)

The core ships reference sources demonstrating two retrieval strategies (§8-§9): FileSystemSource (keyword/full-text) and CSVSource (structured tables, §29). Vector retrieval lives in the optional knowledge layer (KnowledgePipeline + IndexSource) and implements the same Source seam. GitLab / Confluence / S3 and other enterprise systems are domain-specific connectors: application code on top of the Source API (typically under examples/), not core — the framework must not become a catalog of integrations (§61).

docs.title: 8. Retrieval is a Source Capability
docs.text:
The framework must not assume that every Source uses embeddings.

Possible strategies:

Vector search
Keyword search
GitLab API search
Confluence API search
SQL
Filesystem traversal
Regex
AST search
HTTP fetch
Browser navigation
Direct object lookup

A source may use:

ConfluenceSource(
    retrieval="direct_api"
)

while another uses:

MarkdownSource(
    retrieval="vector"
)

and another:

SpreadsheetSource(
    retrieval="sql"
)

The Agent should not care.

The Agent asks for knowledge.

The Source decides how to obtain it.

docs.title: 9. Embeddings are optional
docs.text:
Embeddings are a capability, not an architectural requirement.

The framework must support:

Source A → vector search
Source B → direct API
Source C → SQL
Source D → filesystem
Source E → browser
Source F → GitLab search

A system can therefore combine:

                 Knowledge Runtime
                        │
        ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
        ▼               ▼               ▼
     Vector           Direct          Structured
      Search           API              Query
        │               │               │
        ▼               ▼               ▼
     Markdown       Confluence        XLS/CSV

This is one of the project's deliberate departures from embedding-first RAG.

docs.title: 9.1 Knowledge ingestion is a capability layer, not a second runtime
docs.text:
Turning a corpus into an index is deterministic, linear work:

Connector -> RawDocument -> Document -> Chunk -> EmbeddingProvider -> Index

It is not agent orchestration, and it must not grow a second execution model (graph edges, a YAML workflow DSL, a plugin/type-string registry) inside the framework. The optional reactifact.knowledge layer is therefore:

  • code-first — a connector is an object, configuration is Python;
  • one-way — it may import core protocols and reuse the embedder on RuntimeResources; core never imports it;
  • linear — KnowledgePipeline executes a fixed stage order with incremental DocStore state, not reactive scheduling;
  • bridged explicitly — IndexSource exposes retrieval as a Source, and IngestStep runs ingestion as a Step when an application wants that;
  • observable separately — an optional reactifact.knowledge.web router reads the DocStore run ledger; it is not mixed into RunTrace, which continues to describe agent turns;
  • non-duplicating — answer synthesis, evaluation and tracing stay in quick/recipes/eval/tracing, not in the knowledge layer; the layer exposes a query-time rerank= hook and an optional llm_reranker factory built on the core LLMProvider, while the reranker policy and prompt remain caller-supplied.

Enterprise connectors (GitLab, Confluence, S3, SharePoint, ...) remain application/domain code (§7). The knowledge layer supplies the pipeline, indexes, chunking, incremental state and retrieval mechanics they plug into — not a catalog of integrations (§61).

docs.title: 10. Agent
docs.text:
An Agent is a thin container of Steps. Each step interprets Context and describes a change-set by writing effects (§24); the runtime compiles them into a Patch.

Minimal conceptual interface:

class StepGroup:
    steps: list[Step]

The conceptual "agent" of this document is the public StepGroup; an agent is therefore a group of steps, not a second execution primitive.

An Agent may use:

  • an LLM
  • deterministic code
  • SQL
  • APIs
  • tools
  • other agents
  • external programs
  • statistical methods
  • search
  • tests

An Agent is therefore not synonymous with "LLM".

docs.title: 11. Agent Input and Output Contracts
docs.text:
Agents should declare what they understand.

Example:

class Verifier(Step):
    consumes = (Claim, Evidence)
    produces = (VerifiedClaim, MissingEvidence)

Another:

class DataAnalyst(Step):
    consumes = (Spreadsheet, Hypothesis)
    produces = (Calculation, Finding)

Another:

class Researcher(Step):
    consumes = (Question, Reference)
    produces = (Evidence, Claim)

An Agent groups these steps:

class ResearchFlow(StepGroup):
    steps = [Researcher(), Verifier(), Analyst()]

These declarations are hints and contracts.

They are not necessarily a rigid execution graph.

docs.title: 12. Patch
docs.text:
A Patch is the compiled change-set the runtime applies. The authoring surface is effects (§24): a step writes create/update/delete/link/upsert (or returns Emit/Ensure/Edit/Drop/ Relate) and the runtime compiles the effect set into one atomic Patch (commit, events, validation, trace). Patch is transport — applications rarely build one directly (exceptions: the StepGroup.run escape hatch and advanced assembly).

The compiled operations:

ADD
UPDATE
REMOVE
LINK
UNLINK

Example:

Patch(
    AddArtifact(
        Evidence(
            source=ref,
            content="...",
        )
    ),
    UpdateArtifact(
        claim_id,
        confidence=0.82,
    ),
    Link(
        claim_id,
        evidence_id,
        relation="supported_by",
    ),
)

The runtime validates and applies the patch.

docs.title: 13. Why Changes Are Patches (effects → Patch)
docs.text:
Returning arbitrary objects creates weak composition:

result = agent.run(...)

What does result mean?

How do we:

  • merge it?
  • inspect it?
  • undo it?
  • version it?
  • audit it?
  • compare two agent executions?
  • replay it?
  • detect conflicts?

A Patch solves these problems.

Context v10
     │
     ▼
 Agent
     │
     ▼
 Patch
     │
 ├── ADD Claim
 ├── ADD Evidence
 ├── UPDATE confidence
 └── LINK Claim → Evidence
     │
     ▼
Context v11

docs.title: 14. Immutable Revisions
docs.text:
Artifact handles are immutable snapshots; mutation goes through the Context:

ctx.update(claim.id, claim.data.model_copy(update={"confidence": 0.91}))

Internally, every revision is content-addressed and immutable:

Claim v1
   ↓
Claim v2
   ↓
Claim v3

The Context similarly has versions:

Context v1
Context v2
Context v3
...

This enables:

context.history()
context.diff(v4, v9)
context.checkout(v7)   # move head back; use .at(v) for a detached snapshot
context.snapshot()

The materialized state is an append-only ArtifactStore: ArtifactVersion records carry a canonical payload hash, Context.artifact_version / version_history / find_versions are the canonical historical reads, and persistence v2 writes payloads once in blobs (artifact version index + commit data_ref). Artifact.at/history remain compatibility bridges.

History is bounded, not hoarded forever: a long-lived session collapses old commits into a baseline snapshot (Context.compact(keep_commits=…, keep_versions=…)), preserving the absolute version/head — so context_hash is unchanged — while dropping the operations behind them and trimming each artifact's retained version history. Like squashing git history it is irreversible: checkout/diff below the baseline are refused (Context.compacted_at reports it), and keep_versions is authoritative for the version store.

The initial implementation may use SQLite or another simple persistence layer.

Do not prematurely build a distributed database.

docs.title: 15. Artifact Graph vs Execution Graph
docs.text:
This distinction is one of the central architectural decisions.

An execution graph says:

A → B → C → D

An Artifact Graph says:

Claim
├── supported_by → Evidence
├── derived_from → Document
└── contradicted_by → Evidence

The framework primarily models the second.

Execution may emerge from artifact dependencies and events.

docs.title: 16. Example: Knowledge Chat
docs.text:
Suppose the user asks:

Why did infrastructure costs increase in Q2?

Available sources:

GitLab
Confluence
CSV
XLSX
Markdown
Website

The Context starts as:

Context
└── Question
    └── "Why did infrastructure costs increase in Q2?"

The runtime discovers useful References:

Question
├── GitLabRef
├── ConfluenceRef
├── CSVRef
└── XLSXRef

The researcher materializes selected data:

Evidence
├── Confluence: Infrastructure Costs
├── GitLab MR !1842
├── XLSX: GPU Costs / May
└── CSV: cloud_usage.csv

The analyst creates:

Calculation
└── GPU costs increased by 43%

The investigator creates:

Finding
└── GPU inference workers deployed May 14

The verifier creates:

VerifiedClaim
└── GPU workload growth is strongly associated with Q2 cost increase

The Answer agent produces:

Answer
├── Claim
│   ├── Evidence
│   └── Evidence
├── Claim
│   └── Evidence
└── Confidence

The user receives a human-readable answer.

But internally the answer remains structured.

docs.title: 17. Answer as Artifact
docs.text:
An Answer is not merely:

str

It should contain claims and provenance.

Conceptually:

Answer
├── text
├── claims
│   ├── Claim #1
│   │   ├── Evidence #4
│   │   └── Evidence #8
│   └── Claim #2
│       └── Evidence #12
├── confidence
└── generated_at

This enables a UI such as:

Infrastructure costs increased by 43%.

[Why?]

Evidence:
  XLSX / GPU Costs / May
  GitLab MR !1842
  Confluence / Infrastructure Migration

docs.title: 18. Evidence
docs.text:
Evidence is an explicit Artifact.

It should preserve provenance.

Example:

Evidence(
    source=gitlab_mr,
    location="MR !1842",
    excerpt="...",
)

For spreadsheets:

Evidence(
    source=workbook,
    sheet="Infrastructure",
    range="B182:F214",
)

For Confluence:

Evidence(
    source=page,
    section="GPU Migration",
)

Evidence should point back to the source.

The framework should avoid creating unsupported claims.

docs.title: 19. Claims
docs.text:
A Claim is a proposition that can be evaluated.

Example:

Claim(
    statement="GPU infrastructure costs increased by 43%",
    confidence=0.91,
)

A Claim can have relationships:

Claim
├── supported_by
├── contradicted_by
├── derived_from
└── verified_by

Claims are useful because reasoning becomes inspectable.

docs.title: 20. Hypotheses
docs.text:
A Hypothesis is a candidate explanation.

Example:

Hypothesis A:
GPU workload increased.

Hypothesis B:
Cloud provider pricing changed.

Hypothesis C:
Kubernetes migration increased infrastructure overhead.

The system can investigate these independently.

This gives the runtime a natural way to perform parallel reasoning without requiring the developer to manually build a graph.

docs.title: 21. Reactive Execution
docs.text:
Agents can react to Context changes.

Example:

ClaimAdded
      │
      ▼
Verifier
      │
      ▼
VerifiedClaim
      │
      ▼
Answerer

If evidence is missing:

Verifier
   │
   ▼
MissingEvidence
   │
   ├── GitLabResearcher
   ├── ConfluenceResearcher
   └── WebResearcher

This creates loops naturally:

Research
  ↓
Evidence
  ↓
Claim
  ↓
Verification
  ↓
Missing Evidence
  ↓
Research
  ↺

The loop does not need to be encoded as a graph by the developer.

docs.title: 22. Events
docs.text:
An Event describes a meaningful change.

Examples:

ArtifactCreated
ArtifactUpdated
ArtifactDeleted
ArtifactStale
ClaimCreated
EvidenceAdded
EvidenceMissing
ClaimVerified
ClaimRejected
ConfidenceChanged
TaskBlocked
TaskCompleted

Events are derived from patches or emitted by the runtime.

They can trigger Agents.

docs.title: 23. Runtime
docs.text:
The Runtime coordinates:

  • Context
  • Agents
  • Sources
  • Events
  • Patches
  • scheduling
  • validation
  • persistence
  • observability

Conceptually:

                  Runtime
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       ▼             ▼             ▼
    Context        Agents        Sources
       │             │             │
       │             │             │
       └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                     ▼
                  Scheduler
                     │
                     ▼
            Effects → Patch
                     │
                     ▼
               Context v+1

The Runtime is allowed to use a graph internally.

The public API should not require one.

docs.title: 24. Scheduling Philosophy
docs.text:
The scheduler should answer:

Which Agent has useful work to perform given the current Context?

Not:

Which node is next in my graph?

Possible signals:

Artifact type
Artifact state
Events
Agent capabilities
Missing information
Priority
Budget
Confidence
Dependencies
User intent

Example:

Context:
  4 Claims
  2 unverified
  1 missing evidence

Scheduler:
  Verifier has work
  Researcher has work
  Answerer is blocked

docs.title: 25. Agent Capability Model
docs.text:
Agents should expose capabilities.

Example:

Verifier.capabilities = {
    "verify_claim",
    "detect_contradiction",
}

A Data Analyst:

DataAnalyst.capabilities = {
    "query_table",
    "calculate",
    "aggregate",
    "compare",
}

A Researcher:

Researcher.capabilities = {
    "search_sources",
    "extract_evidence",
    "form_hypothesis",
}

Capabilities can later be used by an LLM planner or deterministic scheduler.

In the shipped runtime the capability contract is declarative and explicit: consumes/produces artifact types (§10-§11, Consume/Step). The scheduler and the LLM router derive work from these declarations, and the runtime validates that an agent only creates artifacts it declared in produces.

docs.title: 26. Deterministic vs LLM Scheduling
docs.text:
The framework should support both.

Deterministic:

if unverified_claim exists:
    run Verifier

LLM-driven:

Given the current Context, decide which capability would most reduce uncertainty.

Hybrid:

                 Scheduler
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
   deterministic         LLM policy
          │                   │
          └─────────┬─────────┘
                    ▼
               Agent choice

The framework should not assume that every orchestration decision requires an LLM.

docs.title: 27. Context Views
docs.text:
Agents should not automatically receive the entire Context.

Instead:

view = context.view(...)

Example:

Researcher sees:
  Question
  References
  relevant metadata

Analyst sees:
  Question
  Spreadsheet
  Hypotheses

Verifier sees:
  Claims
  Evidence
  Source provenance

Answerer sees:
  Verified Claims
  Evidence
  User constraints

This protects token budgets and improves reasoning quality.

docs.title: 28. Context is not Prompt
docs.text:
A Context is structured state.

A Prompt is a serialization of some Context view for a model.

Therefore:

Context
   │
   ▼
Context View
   │
   ▼
Prompt / Tool Calls
   │
   ▼
LLM
   │
   ▼
Patch

The framework should never make the mistake of equating:

Context == prompt string

docs.title: 29. Structured Data Must Remain Structured
docs.text:
For CSV/XLS/XLSX:

Do not default to:

file → chunks → embeddings

Prefer:

Workbook
├── Sheet
│   ├── Schema
│   ├── Row
│   └── Range

Agents may use:

SQL
DuckDB
Pandas
Python
spreadsheet formulas

Example:

table = ctx.get(Spreadsheet, "costs.xlsx")

result = table.query("""
    SELECT month, SUM(gpu_cost)
    FROM costs
    GROUP BY month
""")

The result becomes:

CalculationArtifact

with provenance.

docs.title: 30. Markdown and GitLab
docs.text:
Markdown documents should remain documents.

GitLab entities should remain structured where possible.

Example:

GitLabRepository
├── File
├── Commit
├── MergeRequest
├── Issue
├── Discussion
└── Pipeline

A Markdown file may be materialized as:

MarkdownDocument(
    repository="backend",
    path="docs/auth.md",
    revision="abc123",
)

This allows agents to reason about both content and provenance.

docs.title: 31. Confluence
docs.text:
Confluence should be treated as a live external source.

A page can be:

ConfluencePageRef
        ↓
ConfluencePage
        ↓
Sections
        ↓
Evidence
        ↓
Claims

The framework should support direct access without requiring indexing.

This is a first-class use case, not a fallback.

docs.title: 32. Web / Landing Pages
docs.text:
A website can similarly produce:

WebPageRef
    ↓
WebPage
    ├── title
    ├── sections
    ├── links
    └── content

A source may support:

URL lookup
crawl
search
browser interaction

Again, embedding is optional.

docs.title: 33. Derived Artifacts
docs.text:
Not every Artifact comes from an external Source.

Some are produced by reasoning.

Examples:

Document → Claim
Spreadsheet → Calculation
Claim[] → Finding
Finding[] → Conclusion
Evidence[] → VerifiedClaim
Claims[] → Answer

These are Derived Artifacts.

They should retain provenance:

Calculation
├── derived_from
│   ├── SpreadsheetRange A1:F42
│   └── SpreadsheetRange G1:K42
└── operation
    └── SUM + GROUP BY

docs.title: 34. Provenance is First-Class
docs.text:
Every important derived object should answer:

Why does this exist?

For example:

Answer
  ↓ derived_from
Claim
  ↓ supported_by
Evidence
  ↓ extracted_from
ConfluencePage
  ↓ fetched_from
Confluence API

This creates an evidence graph.

docs.title: 35. Confidence
docs.text:
Confidence belongs to claims and conclusions, not blindly to entire answers.

Example:

Answer
├── Claim A
│   └── confidence = 0.96
├── Claim B
│   └── confidence = 0.72
└── Claim C
    └── confidence = 0.48

The answer can therefore communicate uncertainty precisely.

docs.title: 36. Contradictions
docs.text:
Contradictions are first-class.

Example:

Claim A:
"Migration completed in May."

Evidence:
Confluence → May 12

Contradicting Evidence:
GitLab → final migration commit June 3

The runtime should not silently choose one.

Instead:

Claim
├── supported_by Evidence A
└── contradicted_by Evidence B

A verifier can investigate.

docs.title: 37. Follow-up Questions
docs.text:
A chat session should reuse Context.

Example:

User:
Why did costs increase?

Context v20
   ↓
Answer v20

Then:

User:
How much of that was inference?

Context v21

The new question is added to the existing Context.

Previously materialized artifacts can be reused.

The system should not restart from zero.

docs.title: 38. Incremental Reasoning
docs.text:
A follow-up should only perform necessary work.

Example:

Existing:
GPU costs
GitLab MR
Confluence migration plan

New question:
How much was inference?

Required:
Inference usage data

The runtime should avoid repeating:

GitLab search
Confluence search
GPU calculation

unless evidence is stale or insufficient.

docs.title: 39. Branching
docs.text:
Contexts should be branchable.

branch_a = context.branch()
branch_b = context.branch()

Example:

                   Context v10
                    /       \
                   /         \
          Hypothesis A     Hypothesis B
              │                 │
           research          research
              │                 │
          evidence A        evidence B
                   \         /
                    evaluator
                       │
                       ▼
                  merged state

This is not primarily an execution graph.

It is alternative state exploration.

docs.title: 40. Merge
docs.text:
Branches should be mergeable when changes do not conflict.

Example:

Branch A:
+ Evidence A

Branch B:
+ Evidence B

Merge:
+ Evidence A
+ Evidence B

Conflicting updates must be explicit:

Branch A:
Claim.confidence = 0.8

Branch B:
Claim.confidence = 0.4

Merge conflict

The framework must not silently choose.

Today this is enforced directly: Context.merge() raises MergeConflict and applies nothing when branches touch the same field with different values; resolving it (picking a value, or writing a merge policy) is the caller's responsibility.

A verifier or merge policy can resolve it.

docs.title: 41. Transactions
docs.text:
Patch application should be atomic.

Either:

ADD Claim
ADD Evidence
LINK Claim → Evidence

all succeed,

or the patch does not become visible.

This makes reasoning reproducible.

docs.title: 42. Idempotency
docs.text:
Agents may be retried.

A repeated execution should not create uncontrolled duplicates.

For example:

Researcher runs twice

should not necessarily produce:

Evidence #1
Evidence #2
Evidence #3
Evidence #4

for the same source.

Artifacts should have stable identities. In core, this is unconditional: SourceRef.stable_id() derives an id from sha1(source_id:locator), so re-running a Source against the same locator resolves to the same Artifact rather than creating a duplicate.

Idempotency covers the state, not the environment: a repeated step would still re-send an email. The shipped split is an outbox. A step records an intent artifact — outbox.act(kind=..., key=..., payload=...) creates a PendingAction under the stable id action:{key} — and the runtime performs it after the commit, once per id, through Runtime(dispatcher=...). The step never does the I/O itself. Replay reconstructs the record without running the runtime (so it never re-sends); a retried step re-derives the same id and outbox.act returns None; two branches that independently reach the same action share the id and merge to one intent (§40) — the dispatched side wins, so a merge never re-sends an already-sent action — while divergent payloads under one id are an explicit MergeConflict. The dispatcher receives idempotency_key, so the residual at-least-once window (crash after the send, before the dispatched commit) is closed on the external system's side.

docs.title: 43. Staleness
docs.text:
External artifacts can become stale.

Example:

ConfluencePage
revision=17

Later:

revision=18

The framework should be able to mark:

Artifact:
  stale=True

or materialize a new revision.

Derived claims can then be invalidated or re-evaluated.

docs.title: 44. Invalidations
docs.text:
If a source changes:

Source changed
    ↓
Artifact stale
    ↓
Derived artifacts affected
    ↓
Claims marked stale
    ↓
Verification scheduled

This creates a dependency-aware knowledge system.

docs.title: 45. Memory
docs.text:
Memory should not be a single bucket.

Distinguish:

Context State
Task Artifacts
Persistent Knowledge
Conversation History
Agent Experience
Source Cache

Do not create a vague:

memory = [...]

and put everything there.

docs.title: 46. Tool
docs.text:
A Tool performs an operation.

Examples:

GitLab search
Confluence fetch
SQL query
Python execution
HTTP request
File read

A Tool is not necessarily an Agent.

A useful distinction:

Tool:
"Do this operation."

Agent:
"Decide what operation or reasoning is useful."

An Agent may use tools.

A Source may expose tools.

docs.title: 47. Source vs Tool
docs.text:
Example:

Confluence Source
├── search_pages
├── get_page
└── get_children

These are tools/capabilities of the Source.

An Agent decides:

I need the Authentication Architecture page.

The runtime or agent invokes:

Confluence.get_page(...)

The result becomes an Artifact.

docs.title: 48. Agent Composition
docs.text:
Composition should happen through artifacts.

Not:

agent_a >> agent_b >> agent_c

Prefer:

Agent A
  produces Claim

Agent B
  consumes Claim

Agent C
  consumes VerifiedClaim

The runtime connects them through state.

This allows multiple producers and consumers.

docs.title: 49. One Artifact, Many Agents
docs.text:
Example:

Claim #42
   │
   ├── Verifier
   ├── ContradictionDetector
   ├── Summarizer
   └── Answerer

No explicit graph edge is required.

Each agent declares interest in the Artifact type/state.

docs.title: 50. One Agent, Many Artifact Types
docs.text:
Example:

class DataAnalyst(Step):
    consumes = (Spreadsheet, CSV, Hypothesis)
    produces = (Calculation, Finding)

The runtime creates the relevant Context view.

docs.title: 51. The Agent Should Not Own the State
docs.text:
Bad:

agent.memory = ...
agent.state = ...

Preferred:

Context owns state.
Agent operates on a Context view.
Runtime owns execution.

This makes agents composable.

docs.title: 52. User Interaction
docs.text:
The chat layer should be thin.

Conceptually:

User message
     ↓
Question Artifact
     ↓
Context
     ↓
Runtime
     ↓
Agents
     ↓
Artifacts
     ↓
Answer Artifact
     ↓
UI

The UI should render structured artifacts.

docs.title: 53. Streaming
docs.text:
The runtime should be able to stream events:

Searching GitLab...
Found MR !1842
Reading Confluence page...
Analyzing spreadsheet...
Verified claim...
Generating answer...

These are runtime events, not necessarily LLM tokens.

The UI can separately stream model output.

docs.title: 54. Observability
docs.text:
Every meaningful operation should be inspectable.

At minimum:

Run
Agent
Input Context version
Output Patch
Tool calls
Artifacts created
Artifacts modified
Latency
Tokens
Cost
Errors

Example:

Run #184

Agent: Verifier
Context: v47
Duration: 8.2s

Reads:
  Claim #12
  Evidence #91
  Evidence #93

Produces:
  Claim #12 v4

Patch:
  confidence 0.72 → 0.91

This is essential for debugging agent systems.

docs.title: 55. Replay
docs.text:
Given:

Context v20
Agent execution
Patch

the system should eventually support replay.

This allows:

Why did the agent produce this answer?

to be answered concretely.

Replay is state reconstruction, not re-execution: it walks the commit chain and rebuilds the Context without running agents, so outbound side effects recorded as PendingActions (§42) are read back as state, not re-sent. replay_summary reports their dispatched/pending/failed counts.

docs.title: 56. Evaluation
docs.text:
Because state is structured, evaluation can happen at multiple levels.

Instead of only:

answer == expected_answer

evaluate:

Evidence quality
Claim correctness
Provenance correctness
Calculation correctness
Confidence calibration
Answer quality
Source coverage

Example:

Research quality: 0.91
Claim verification: 0.96
Calculation: 1.00
Final answer: 0.89

docs.title: 57. Security
docs.text:
Status: planned, not yet implemented. The rules below describe the target design — no Artifact currently carries owner/permissions/classification, and Context views do not yet enforce access control.

Artifacts may contain sensitive information.

Every Artifact should eventually support:

owner
permissions
source
classification
visibility

A Context view should enforce access control.

An Agent must not receive artifacts it is not allowed to see.

docs.title: 58. Cost and Budget
docs.text:
Budget belongs to Runtime, not directly to the LLM.

Shipped dimensions (reactifact.budget.Budget):

Budget(
    max_runs=...,          # agent runs
    max_iterations=...,    # loop generations
    max_seconds=...,       # wall clock
    max_tool_calls=...,    # tool executions (LLM agents)
    max_tokens=...,        # total prompt + completion over the turn
    max_cost=...,          # over the turn, via an injected Pricer
)

Exhaustion is an outcome, not an exception (RunOutcome): budget_runs_exceeded, budget_time_exceeded, budget_tokens_exceeded, budget_cost_exceeded, iterations_exhausted. The runtime may terminate or downgrade expensive strategies.

Token/cost usage is counted by the runtime itself — a BudgetTracker filled by a BudgetLLM proxy over resources.llm — independent of tracing, which is optional; RunStats reports the totals. Streaming is counted too (a chunk's usage, when the provider reports it). A call is allowed to finish: the budget stops the next generation or loop step, so a run can overshoot by at most one call. Cost needs an injected Pricer (reactifact.pricing); the framework ships no built-in price table.

docs.title: 59. Failure Model
docs.text:
Failures should become state, not just exceptions.

Examples:

ToolFailed
SourceUnavailable
EvidenceMissing
ArtifactInvalid
AgentFailed
VerificationFailed
BudgetExceeded

Some failures should trigger recovery.

Example:

Confluence unavailable
       ↓
SourceUnavailable
       ↓
Try cached artifact
       ↓
Try GitLab
       ↓
Report uncertainty

docs.title: 60. Human-in-the-loop
docs.text:
Humans should interact with Context and Artifacts.

Possible operations:

Approve Claim
Reject Claim
Edit Artifact
Add Evidence
Resolve Conflict
Approve Action

Human changes should produce normal Patches.

This keeps the state model unified.

docs.title: 61. What the Framework Is Not
docs.text: The project is not:

docs.title: Another LangChain
docs.text: It does not primarily provide a large catalog of integrations.

docs.title: Another LangGraph
docs.text: It does not require users to describe execution as a graph.

docs.title: Another CrewAI
docs.text: It does not primarily model teams of role-playing agents.

docs.title: Another DSPy
docs.text: It does not primarily optimize prompts/programs.

docs.title: Another vector database
docs.text: Embeddings are optional.

docs.title: Another workflow engine
docs.text: Workflows may exist internally, but they are not the central developer abstraction.

docs.title: 62. Relationship to Existing Frameworks
docs.text:
A conceptual comparison:

System Primary abstraction LangChain Chains, tools, agents LangGraph Explicit stateful graph CrewAI Role-based multi-agent collaboration DSPy Optimizable LM programs This framework Evolving typed Context + Artifacts

The goal is not to prove that the new abstraction is universally better.

The goal is to make it especially strong for:

  • knowledge agents
  • enterprise assistants
  • research agents
  • coding agents
  • data analysis
  • multi-source investigation
  • long-running reasoning
  • artifact-producing agents

docs.title: 63. Design Rule: Prefer State Semantics Over Execution Semantics
docs.text:
When designing an API, ask:

Can this be expressed as a property of Context and Artifacts?

before asking:

Which node should run next?

Example.

Instead of:

graph.add_edge(
    researcher,
    verifier
)

prefer:

class Verifier(Step):
    consumes = (UnverifiedClaim,)

The runtime derives execution.

docs.title: 64. Design Rule: Preserve Information Structure
docs.text:
Do not flatten structured data unnecessarily.

Prefer:

Spreadsheet → Table → Range

over:

Spreadsheet → Text chunks

Prefer:

GitLab MR → commits → files

over:

GitLab MR → text chunk

Prefer:

Confluence Page → sections

over:

Confluence Page → embedding

Embeddings can coexist with structure.

They should not destroy it.

docs.title: 65. Design Rule: Every Derived Artifact Should Have Provenance
docs.text:
If an agent creates:

Finding

we should eventually be able to answer:

What created it?
From which artifacts?
Using which tools?
At which Context version?

This is mandatory for trustworthy systems.

docs.title: 66. Design Rule: Agents Should Be Replaceable
docs.text:
A Context should not depend on a specific LLM.

This should be possible:

GPT Agent
   ↓
Patch

and:

Claude Agent
   ↓
Patch

and:

Local Model Agent
   ↓
Patch

If they respect the same contracts, the Runtime should not care.

docs.title: 67. Design Rule: Deterministic Work Should Not Use an LLM
docs.text:
If something can be safely done with deterministic code:

CSV aggregation
JSON parsing
schema validation
diff
sorting
filtering
SQL

do not require an LLM.

The LLM should handle ambiguity, interpretation, planning, and reasoning.

docs.title: 68. Design Rule: The LLM Should Not Own Truth
docs.text:
The model may propose:

Claim

but the system should preserve:

Evidence
Provenance
Verification
Confidence

The model is a reasoning component, not the source of truth.

docs.title: 69. Design Rule: Make Illegal States Visible
docs.text:
If an Answer contains a Claim with no Evidence, this should be detectable.

If a Calculation references a deleted Spreadsheet Range, this should be detectable.

If a Claim is contradicted, this should be represented.

Do not hide these conditions inside strings.

docs.title: 70. Design Rule: Prefer Explicit Uncertainty
docs.text:
Bad:

The migration caused the increase.

Better internal representation:

Claim:
  statement = "Migration caused the increase"
  confidence = 0.61
  supported_by = [...]
  contradicted_by = [...]

The UI may still render a concise answer.

docs.title: 71. Initial Python API
docs.text:
The primary programming model, as shipped in 0.24:

from pydantic import BaseModel

from reactifact import (
    Artifact,
    Budget,
    Context,
    Effects,
    Runtime,
    RuntimeResources,
    Step,
    StepGroup,
)
from reactifact.sources import FileSystemSource, SourceRef


class Question(BaseModel):
    text: str


ctx = Context(
    resources=RuntimeResources(
        sources={"docs": FileSystemSource("./docs")},
    )
)
ctx.create(Question(text="How is authentication implemented?"))

Agents are thin containers (§48): all logic lives in Step classes that write effects.create/update/delete/link/upsert (or return a model); the runtime compiles the effects into one Patch. consumes/produces on each step are the artifact contracts that drive the scheduler:

class Researcher(Step):
    consumes = (Question, SourceRef)
    produces = (Evidence,)

    async def run(
        self, question: Question, ref: Artifact[SourceRef], effects: Effects
    ) -> None:
        ...  # writes effects.create/update/delete/link/upsert


class Verifier(Step):
    consumes = (Evidence,)
    produces = (VerifiedClaim,)

    async def run(self, evidence: Evidence, effects: Effects) -> None:
        ...


class Answerer(Step):
    consumes = (VerifiedClaim,)
    produces = (Answer,)

    async def run(self, claim: VerifiedClaim, effects: Effects) -> None:
        ...


class ResearcherAgent(StepGroup):
    name = "researcher"
    steps = [Researcher(), Verifier(), Answerer()]


runtime = Runtime(
    ctx,
    groups=[ResearcherAgent(), VerifierAgent(), AnswererAgent()],
    budget=Budget(max_runs=80),
)
runtime.run()

Step.run in the framework's terminology is the work unit: interpret a relevant Context view, describe changes via effects, and let the runtime compile + apply them.

docs.title: 72. Target Knowledge Chat API
docs.text:
As built in examples/knowledge (imports elided — they mirror the demo):

resources = RuntimeResources(
    llm=llm,
    sources={
        "guide": FileSystemSource("./docs/guide"),
        "pricing": FileSystemSource("./docs/pricing"),
        "costs": CSVSource("./docs/costs"),  # §29: structure, not text
    },
)
session = SessionStore(FileKVBackend("./sessions")).open("knowledge", resources=resources)

runtime = Runtime(
    session.context,
    groups=[
        Planner(), SearchScout(), ResolverAgent(), TableResolver(),
        EvidenceBuilder(), VerifierAgent(), CalculatorAgent(),
        ProgressEvaluator(), AnswerBuilder(),
    ],
    budget=Budget(max_runs=80),
)

query = session.context.create(UserQuery(text="Why did infrastructure costs increase in Q2?"))
runtime.run()

The developer does not describe a graph. Agents react to artifact types (Consume), and the runtime derives execution from state changes. The chat layer is thin (§52): a question enters the Context, agents produce evidence and verified claims, an answer emerges with provenance.

docs.title: 73. Internal Execution Example
docs.text:
The user sees:

Why did infrastructure costs increase in Q2?

Infrastructure costs increased by 43%, primarily due to
increased GPU inference workloads introduced during Q2.

Internally:

Question #1
   ↓
References discovered
   ↓
ConfluencePage #18
GitLabMR #1842
Spreadsheet #77
   ↓
Evidence #91
Evidence #92
Evidence #93
   ↓
Calculation #12
   ↓
Hypothesis #7
   ↓
Claim #22
   ↓
Verification
   ↓
VerifiedClaim #23
   ↓
Answer #5

docs.title: Phase 1 — Core state model
docs.text:
Implement only:

Artifact
Reference
Context
Patch
Revision

No autonomous agents.

Goal:

create → update → diff → rollback

docs.title: Phase 2 — Reference sources
docs.text:
Reference sources shipped in the core, each demonstrating a retrieval strategy (§8-§9):

Filesystem   keyword / full-text  (FileSystemSource)
CSV          structured tables    (CSVSource → Spreadsheet/Calculation)

Vector retrieval is not a core Source: use the optional knowledge layer
(KnowledgePipeline + IndexSource) or a custom Source subclass.

Goal:

Reference → Artifact

Support lazy resolution.

GitLab, Confluence and similar enterprise systems are domain-specific connectors: application code on top of the Source API (typically under examples/), so the core does not accumulate a catalog of integrations.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Step / StepGroup contract
docs.text:
Implement:

Step.run(...) -> Model | None             # writes effects.*; runtime compiles
# Effects(create/update/delete/link/upsert) -▶ Patch: the atomic change
# plus the thin StepGroup container: a list of Steps

Add:

StepGroup.steps
Step.consumes
Step.produces

docs.title: Phase 4 — Reactive Runtime
docs.text:
Implement:

Event
Scheduler
Agent selection
Patch application

Goal:

Artifact changes → relevant Agent executes

docs.title: Phase 5 — Knowledge Chat
docs.text:
Implement:

Question
Research
Evidence
Claim
Verification
Answer

Goal:

Ask a question over GitLab + Confluence + files and receive an evidence-backed answer.

docs.title: Phase 6 — Structured data
docs.text:
Add:

CSV
XLS
XLSX
DuckDB
Python execution

Goal:

Agents can calculate instead of hallucinating calculations.

docs.title: Phase 7 — Provenance and UI
docs.text:
Add:

Evidence graph
Artifact history
Diff
Sources
Claim inspection

docs.title: Phase 8 — Branching and advanced reasoning
docs.text:
Add:

Context branching
Parallel hypotheses
Merge
Conflict resolution

docs.title: Phase 9 — Adaptive scheduler
docs.text:
Add:

budget
priority
uncertainty reduction
LLM scheduling

Only after the core model is proven.

docs.title: 75. What Not to Build First
docs.text:
Do not start with:

Multi-agent teams
Long-term memory
Vector database
Autonomous planning
Browser agents
Distributed execution
Complex DAG engine
Agent marketplace
Fine-tuning

These are secondary.

The first question is:

Is Context + Artifact + Patch genuinely a better primitive for building agents?

Everything else depends on this answer.

docs.title: 76. First Technical Prototype
docs.text:
The first prototype should be able to execute this:

ctx = Context(resources=RuntimeResources(sources={...}))

question = ctx.create(Question(text="Why did costs increase?"))

ctx.create(ConfluencePageRef(...))
ctx.create(GitLabFileRef(...))
ctx.create(SpreadsheetRef(...))

runtime.run(ctx)

And produce:

Context v0
    Question
    References

Context v1
    Documents

Context v2
    Evidence
    Claims

Context v3
    Calculations
    Findings

Context v4
    Verified Claims

Context v5
    Answer

Then:

ctx.history()

should show the evolution.

docs.title: 77. The First Demo Should Be Extremely Concrete
docs.text:
Use one real problem:

"Why did our infrastructure costs increase in Q2?"

Provide:

GitLab:
  docs/
  merge requests
  commits

Confluence:
  architecture documentation

CSV:
  cloud costs

XLSX:
  infrastructure budget

The system should:

  1. understand the question;
  2. locate relevant sources;
  3. lazily materialize only useful artifacts;
  4. extract evidence;
  5. calculate values from structured data;
  6. form hypotheses;
  7. verify claims;
  8. produce an answer;
  9. show provenance.

If this works elegantly, the architecture is validated.

docs.title: 79. The Core Mental Model
docs.text:
When designing a new feature, think in this order:

1. What Artifact does this represent?
2. What is its provenance?
3. Who can create it?
4. Who can modify it?
5. What makes it valid?
6. What events does its creation/update produce?
7. Which Agents can consume it?
8. Which Agents can produce derived artifacts?
9. What happens if the source changes?
10. How can we inspect and reproduce the result?

Do not start with:

Which node should I add?

docs.title: 80. Final Constitution
docs.text: The project follows these foundational principles:

docs.title: Principle 1
docs.text: State is primary. Execution is derived.

docs.title: Principle 2
docs.text: Artifacts are first-class.

docs.title: Principle 3
docs.text: References and materialized Artifacts are different things.

docs.title: Principle 4
docs.text: External knowledge does not have to be embedded.

docs.title: Principle 5
docs.text: Agents transform Context through Patches.

docs.title: Principle 6
docs.text: Context is versioned.

docs.title: Principle 7
docs.text: Derived information preserves provenance.

docs.title: Principle 8
docs.text: Structured data remains structured.

docs.title: Principle 9
docs.text: The LLM is a reasoning component, not the source of truth.

docs.title: Principle 10
docs.text: Deterministic computation should remain deterministic.

docs.title: Principle 11
docs.text: Uncertainty and contradictions are explicit state.

docs.title: Principle 12
docs.text: Agents should react to state rather than require manually authored execution graphs.

docs.title: Principle 13
docs.text: The framework may use graphs internally, but graphs are not the primary developer abstraction.

docs.title: Principle 14
docs.text: Every important decision should be explainable through Context history, Artifacts, Events, and Patches.

docs.title: Principle 15
docs.text: The simplest useful system is the goal; sophistication must emerge from the primitives rather than from framework ceremony.

docs.title: 81. One-Sentence Definition
docs.text:
If the project needs a single sentence:

A framework for building agents as reactive, stateful processes that transform versioned, typed, provenance-aware Artifacts inside an evolving Context.

And the shortest mental model is:

                 AGENT
                   │
                   ▼
             ┌───────────┐
             │  CONTEXT  │
             └─────┬─────┘
                   │
                 PATCH
                   │
                   ▼
             ┌───────────┐
             │  CONTEXT' │
             └───────────┘

Everything else — tools, RAG, APIs, planners, schedulers, multi-agent execution, memory, verification, branching — is built around these primitives.

docs.title: Appendix — Implementation Status
docs.text:
State of the public reactifact codebase at 0.25.1 (pre-1.0). Verification: ~1700 tests (optional-dependency skips in a bare venv); mypy strict, ruff, import-linter and the docs build are clean.

Area Section(s) Status Context / Artifact / Patch / Revision (git-like) §4, §12, §14 implemented — Artifact is a frozen handle over an append-only ArtifactStore; artifact_version/version_history/find_versions are canonical; Demos shipped in the repo (not in the wheel):

  • examples/knowledge — multi-source chat: search → evidence → claim verification → answer, plus CSV calculation and a web dashboard.
  • examples/medic_lab — hypothesis laboratory: competing hypotheses, deterministic scoring, HITL steering, honest report.
  • examples/devops — ops assistant: HITL tool agents, LLM tool router, run-trace dashboard with auth.
  • examples/repair — budget-aware replanning demo. Its chat and data are intentionally Russian (a deliberate product choice, §68-adjacent); code and comments are English.
  • examples/forklab — branch/merge state exploration (§39-40).
  • examples/fintech_audit — auditable CSV answer with content hashes.
  • examples/knowledge_base — code-first connector → chunks → index ingestion and hybrid retrieval over a real corpus.
  • examples/code_review — deterministic diff rules plus optional LLM findings.
  • examples/outbox — committed side effects, retry and replay.
  • examples/repo_agent — a destructive tool behind an approval gate.
  • examples/starter_app — copy-pasteable FastAPI app over the quick cases.
  • examples/chat — minimal offline multi-turn chat.
  • examples/tour — small scenes for the framework primitives.
  • examples/approval_gate.py — a standalone approval-intent walkthrough.

The full catalog is in Examples.

Roadmap direction: the 0.24 line lands the CLI/daemon/HTTP adapters, knowledge connectors and lifecycle consumes; next is the 1.0 surface freeze (no new breaking changes), stronger adaptive scheduling, and more Source integrations (SQL, keyword search) as the concrete gaps.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: reactifact is pre-1.0, one maintainer. This page is the honest current state of "what's next" — not a wishlist. See CHANGELOG.md for what's already shipped, release by release.

docs.title: Now
docs.text:
• Finish the Step-era API. The reactive core is being consolidated around Step/@step, step-owned consumes/produces, explicit effects: Effects, typed inputs (Artifact[T], list[Artifact[T]], Annotated[T, When(...)], Latest[T]) and StepGroup.steps. 0.24 removed the last 0.x Agent aliases; the goal is one obvious way to write a unit of work.
  • Content-addressed artifact state. Artifact is a frozen handle over an append-only ArtifactStore; Context.artifact_version / version_history / find_versions are canonical, persistence is v2 (blobs + version index + commit data_ref), and compaction is authoritative. Remaining work is closing compatibility edges and docs.
  • Keep the example set small. The repo keeps the reference applications (devops, knowledge, forklab, repair, medic_lab, fintech_audit, starter_app, chat) instead of maintaining every historical pattern demo.
  • MCP hardening (more transport coverage, more real-server testing) before adding new integration surfaces.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Stable 1.0 — freeze the public API surface, commit to semver guarantees, and close out breaking changes before they accumulate further. The surface has three stability tiers:
  • Core (frozen hardest): Context/Artifact (frozen handle + version store)/Effects/Patch/Step/StepGroup/Source/Provenance/HITL (PendingQuestion, human.ask/resume), plus RuntimeResources's own extension points — context_builder (reactifact.context_builder) and verification_threshold (reactifact.verify) count as core because they're config surface on a core object, not a separable add-on.
  • "In the box" (stable, evolves faster than core): Tool/ToolUse/ ToolUseHITL (including the destructive-tool approval gate), reactifact.tools.native, reactifact.tools.agent.AgentAsTool, verify.Verify's metric surface, MCP, tracing/observability, providers. Same semver discipline, a lower bar for additive capability.

  • Recipes (reactifact.recipes, docs/en/recipes.md) — frozen at 1.0, explicitly the layer meant to keep growing fastest post-1.0; new recipes are additive, framework-internal moves stay off their public surface.

  • More Source integrations — today's built-in sources are filesystem, CSV, embeddings and WebSource (see the knowledge example). The Source protocol (reactifact/sources.py) is intentionally small so this grows by adding implementations, not by changing the abstraction: direct API sources, SQL and keyword search are the concrete gaps.

docs.title: Non-goals (for now)
docs.text:
Carried over from docs/en/comparison.md — worth repeating here since a roadmap page is where people look for the opposite promise:

  • No managed hosting / SaaS platform. reactifact is a library; there is no hosted execution or UI for non-engineers planned.
  • No large pre-built agent/tool marketplace. The Source and MCP abstractions stay small and composable rather than growing a plugin ecosystem to compete on integration count.

docs.title: Contributing to the direction
docs.text: Roadmap changes and feature discussion happen in GitHub Discussions, not silently in code. If something here looks wrong or missing, open one.

docs.title: reactifact
docs.text:
Auditable agents for Python. Build knowledge assistants over docs, spreadsheets and the web — where the path per question isn't a graph you can draw. Every answer is computed, versioned and reproducible — not a string you have to trust.

Is: a Python library (3 core deps) · single-process · typed, versioned artifacts with provenance · deterministic replay · runs offline, no API key Isn't: a managed platform · a distributed task queue · a pre-built agent/tool marketplace

A question like "why did infra costs jump in Q2?" needs a spreadsheet, a policy doc and a page off the web — and the next question needs a different subset. That is not one graph you can draw up front. You declare what artifacts exist and what agents can do with them; the runtime derives the order — and the dependency graph — from state. You don't draw the graph. Every derived artifact then links to what produced it (Answer —supported_by→ Evidence —extracted_from→ Doc), so "why did it say that?" is a query, not a guess — and the run is reproducible (context_hash) and verifiable (reactifact replay --verify).

If you know Celery… — the programming model, not its distributed runtime Python developers already know this model from Celery: define a **task**, declare what triggers it, let the runtime run it. `reactifact` applies it to agents: a task reacts to a **typed, versioned artifact** in the context, not to a queued message or a graph edge. | Celery | reactifact | | --- | --- | | a task | `Step` / `@step(produces=Model, consumes=Input)` — a unit of work that writes an artifact | | `delay()` / `apply_async()` | you don't call it: creating the input artifact **is** the trigger | | routing key / queue | `Consume(Type)` — which artifact type wakes the task | | chain / group / chord | several step `Consume`s / `produces`; the runtime derives the order | | result backend | the `Context` — typed, versioned artifacts | | worker | `Runtime` | **Not inherited:** a broker, a worker pool, `acks_late`/redelivery, cross-process exactly-once — the *model* is Celery-shaped, the deployment is not.
