Artifact payloads are content-addressed in the snapshot: blobs stores each payload once under (data_type, content_hash), artifact entries hold a version index, and commit Create/Update operations reference the same blobs via data_ref. ctx.artifact_version() / version_history() / find_versions() read that store; Artifact.at/history remain compatibility bridges. The payload carries a format_version; a payload from a newer reactifact is rejected explicitly, older ones (including v1 inline history) go through the registered migrations (Context.from_dict).

With an AppendBackend (SQLiteKVBackend, PostgreSQLKVBackend) the store does not rewrite the whole Context on every commit: the first save (or the first save after a compaction/checkout) writes a snapshot, and later saves append only the new commits plus the current pending-event queue. FileKVBackend and InMemoryKVBackend keep the full-blob behavior.

SessionStore(backend, compact_every=N) bounds the append log: roughly every N saves the store rewrites the snapshot and clears the entries. The default is 100; pass compact_every=None to keep the log until an explicit context.compact() or a checkout. BranchStore takes the same option per branch key.

With the default session_save_policy="per_commit", the runtime saves at every generation boundary, after that generation's trigger batch is consumed. So the saved snapshot is consistent: an already-consumed trigger is not replayed, and one whose consumer never ran is.

from reactifact import Runtime, SessionStore
from reactifact.checkpoints import SQLiteKVBackend

store = SessionStore(SQLiteKVBackend("sessions.sqlite3"))
session = await store.open("user-1")            # loads, or creates if absent
runtime = Runtime(session.context, groups=[...], session=session)
await runtime.arun()

# after a crash / restart — a brand-new process, nothing in memory
session = await store.open("user-1")
runtime = Runtime(session.context, groups=[...], session=session)
await runtime.arun()   # continues: pending triggers are still there

A crashed run therefore resumes from the last committed generation, and any trigger that was queued but not yet reacted to is re-dispatched.

docs.title: The guarantee: at-least-once
docs.text:
Resume is at-least-once, not exactly-once. A step that had already committed before the crash may run again. If it is not idempotent, that means a duplicate artifact (or a repeated external side effect).

Give steps a stable id so a re-run upserts instead of duplicating (§42):

@step(produces=Summary, consumes=Msg)
async def summarize(call):
    doc = call.trigger
    # A stable id makes the re-run idempotent: creating it twice returns the
    # same artifact and emits no second event.
    call.effects.create(Summary(text=...), id=f"summary:{doc.data.url}")

effects.create_once_from(...) (stable id derived from the trigger) and Consume(..., debounce=True) are the other tools for the same goal.

docs.title: What is not covered
docs.text:
• External side effects inside a step. An email, a file write, or a third-party API call made directly in a step can be repeated by a retry. Do not do that — record an intent instead: outbox.act(kind=..., key=..., payload=...) writes a PendingAction and Runtime(dispatcher=...) performs it once after the intent commits (see the outbox pattern in Patterns). The framework still cannot make the I/O itself exactly-once — the dispatcher must be idempotent on idempotency_key (passed through in action.data), which closes the residual at-least-once window. (call.request is available for a correlation id; see reactifact.request.)
  • No background relay. The framework never runs a process that keeps retrying the outbox on its own: the next arun() drains committed actions, and flush_pending_actions() drains them without a generation — call it on startup and periodically (in your app's own timer) so an action committed just before a crash is not stranded. Retry policy is the application's: a failing dispatcher marks the action failed (bumping attempts), fires Runtime(on_dispatch_error=...) if set, and re-raises; context.retry_action( id) re-arms it.
  • In-flight work. A step that was mid-flight at the crash is simply re-run; only committed generations are durable.
  • Budgets reset per run. Budget counters (max_runs, max_seconds) are per-arun() call; resuming starts a fresh budget, not the remainder of the old one.
  • per_turn granularity. With session_save_policy="per_turn" the session is saved once at the end of a turn, so a crash mid-turn rolls the whole turn back and re-runs it. per_commit (default) saves at every generation boundary instead.

docs.title: Outbox in production
docs.text:
The outbox primitive is safe by construction, but it is a library feature, not a delivery service: it runs no relay and invents no retry policy. To ship outbound effects (email, webhooks, payments) in production you own four things:

  1. An idempotent dispatcher. Pass action.data.idempotency_key to the external system so the at-least-once window (a crash between the send and the dispatched commit) is closed on the far side. Never mint a new key on a retry.
  2. A drain. Call flush_pending_actions() on startup and periodically from your own timer, so an action committed just before a crash is not stranded. The next arun() drains too — but only if a turn actually runs.
  3. A retry policy. A failing dispatcher marks the action failed (bumping attempts) and re-raises; wrap your dispatcher with your own retry/backoff, and/or hook Runtime(on_dispatch_error=...) to alert and context.retry_action(id) to re-arm. Backoff is deliberately not in the runtime.
  4. Observability. Query context.list_artifacts(PendingAction) (or the replay CLI) for failed and long-pending actions and alert on them.

With those four in place it is production-ready; if you want the framework itself to keep retrying with no app timer, that is a broker/relay — out of scope by design (§75). Implement the dispatcher-level retry wrapper in the app.

docs.title: Schema evolution
docs.text:
A persisted artifact's type is stored as a string (Artifact.data_type, the data_type of a compiled Create/Update, Event.artifact_type) — by default the Python qualified name (module.Qualname). You do not have to register anything: on save the id is derived automatically, and on load resolve imports the qualified name back, so a normal module-level model round-trips with no boilerplate. reactifact.types exists only to decouple that stored identity from Python's module layout when you want to.

Registration matters in three cases:

  • Renames or moves — a stable type_id keeps old sessions/recordings loadable after a model is renamed or moved between modules.
  • Aliases — payloads carrying a previous id keep resolving.
  • Schema migration — a migrate hook renames fields / fills defaults before validation.
from reactifact import register_type

register_type(
    Answer,
    type_id="answer",                                   # written from now on
    aliases=["old.pkg.Answer"],                         # what old payloads carry
    migrate=lambda d: {**d, "prose": d.pop("text", "")},  # a field rename
)

When you only need a stable id (no aliases/migration), a TYPE_ID classvar on the model is enough — no call needed. Call register_type at import time, next to the model.

  • type_id_of(model) — the id written on save: a registered type_id, a TYPE_ID classvar, else the qualified name.
  • resolve(type_id) — the class on load: registry → alias → import by qualified name, so pre-registry payloads keep loading.
  • migrate runs on the raw dict before validation (field renames, defaults).

The one real caveat: a qualified name is only loadable if the class is importable in the new process. A model defined in __main__, in a notebook cell, inside a function (<locals>), or built with pydantic.create_model is not — its id will not resolve on resume/replay. Give such a model an explicit type_id (and a real module to live in); resolve's error names the id it could not find and points at register.

This covers artifacts, commit operations and events — a whole session's state and its pending trigger queue — so an upgrade that renames/moves a model no longer breaks resume, replay or golden snapshots.

docs.title: Resume vs. replay
docs.text:
Two different operations, often confused:

  • Resume (session.open(...) + Runtime.arun()) continues an interrupted run: it re-dispatches pending triggers and may re-run produces.
  • Replay (reactifact replay, ReplayLLM) reconstructs why a completed run reached its state, deterministically, without re-running agents — see Replay.

The first is execution; the second is audit.

docs.title: Checkpoints and forks
docs.text:
Each commit is also a lightweight checkpoint. context.checkpoints() returns them oldest-to-head (id, version, author, message, writes); context.checkpoint(id_or_version) resolves one, and context.at(checkpoint) gives a detached snapshot without rewinding the live context.

To start an independent session from a past state:

history = context.checkpoints()
fork = await store.fork("s1", new_id="s1-try2", at=history[-2])
# fork.context is the state at that checkpoint; the source session is untouched

Without at=, the current state is copied (including the pending trigger queue); with at=, pending events/step cursors are cleared — a clean time-travel base. store.checkpoints("s1") lists them without opening a Session. reactifact replay <store> --at <commit-id> does the read-only variant from the CLI.

docs.title: Deadlines, graceful shutdown & in-flight runs
docs.text:
Budget.max_seconds is enforced as a hard per-turn deadline: the runtime cancels the generation in flight (a hung LLM call is actually stopped) rather than only checking between generations. The cancelled generation's trigger batch is not consumed, so a later arun() resumes it; the turn ends with RunOutcome.BUDGET_TIME_EXCEEDED.

On process shutdown, Runtime.request_stop() asks the run to stop at the next generation boundary — the current generation finishes (its commit lands), no new one starts, and RunOutcome.STOPPED is set. await runtime.ashutdown(timeout=…) does that and waits for the turn, force-cancelling after timeout. It never closes shared RuntimeResources; close those in your own lifespan (resources.aclose() or a ResourceScope).

The process's in-flight turns are visible read-only:

from reactifact.runtime import active_runs, cancel_run

len(active_runs())           # a readiness signal
active_runs()[0].session_id  # what is running
cancel_run(run_id)           # cancel one turn

active_runs() is in-process only — single event loop, not persisted, not cross-process. It is an ops/readiness view, not a task queue.

docs.title: Bounding a long-lived context
docs.text:
A session that lives for many turns keeps every commit and every artifact version forever — memory (and to_dict) grows without bound. Context.compact bounds it the way git squashes history:

session.context.compact(keep_commits=50, keep_versions=2)

It collapses every commit older than the last keep_commits into a baseline snapshot and (with keep_versions) trims each artifact's retained version history. The absolute version/head_id are preserved, so context_hash, commit version numbers and resumes are unaffected.

Two honest consequences:

  • It is irreversible. checkout/diff below the resulting baseline raise (Context.compacted_at reports it), and provenance for artifacts last written before the baseline is gone — the operations that produced them were collapsed.
  • It does not evict artifacts. To drop old artifacts (e.g. out-of-window messages), use the memory recipes (WindowPruner, RollingDigestSummarizer, Recipes); compact bounds the history, not the working set.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Execution model — the generation loop and its explicit non-guarantees.
  • Concepts — Context, commits, and the event queue.
  • Replay — verifying a finished run's context_hash.

docs.title: The step contract & effects (§24)
docs.text:
One paragraph to keep in your head while reading any example or writing a step:

A step describes what should change by writing effects, or returns its output; the runtime compiles the change-set into one atomic patch and commits it. You almost never build a Patch yourself — it is the runtime's transport.

from reactifact import Artifact, Effects, Human

async def run(
    self,
    doc: Artifact[Document],
    turn: Artifact[Turn],
    effects: Effects,
    human: Human,
) -> None:
    evidence = effects.create(Evidence(...), id="evidence:q1")
    answer = effects.create(Answer(...), id="answer:q1")
    evidence.link("extracted_from", doc)
    answer.link("supported_by", evidence)
    effects.update(turn, status="answered")
    human.ask("Approve the estimate?", kind="approval")   # HITL (§60)

A class step that writes effects declares an effects: Effects parameter in run() — the runtime injects the step-scoped slot. A @step function receives the single call: StepCall argument and writes call.effects; both reach the same effect set, just through a different surface (the function form has no self).

Inputs can be selected inline: Annotated[T, When(...)] conditions a type. An explicit consumes is the wake set, so typed artifact params not listed there are read-only inputs automatically — no wakes=False needed. When consumes is derived from the signature, Annotated[T, Wakes(False)] marks one read-only input (history: Annotated[ConversationHistory, Wakes(False)]). For debounce, custom event types, or subclass matching, use Consume(...) explicitly.

scope correlates typed inputs. scope = "query_id" is the shorthand; when a correlated artifact is identified by its id rather than a data field, name the owner:

scope = Scope("question_id", owner=Question)

Now Question matches by artifact.id, while Hypothesis/Evidence/Claim match by data.question_id. Scope(..., key=fn) supplies a custom extractor when the key lives in notes (e.g. a PendingQuestion).

docs.title: Return vs effects
docs.text:
Returning a model (or a list of models) is create-sugar:

async def run(self, question: Artifact[Question]) -> Answer:
    return Answer(text=question.data.text)

When the id or provenance must be explicit, return Emit instead of dropping to effects:

from reactifact import Emit

return Emit(
    Answer(text=...),
    id=f"answer:{question.id}",
    links=(("supported_by", evidence),),
)

Emit with an id that already exists refreshes the artifact (the upsert equivalent). When an existing artifact should be left untouched, return Ensure instead:

from reactifact import Ensure

return Ensure(Answer(text=...), source=question, prefix="answer")
# or: Ensure(Answer(text=...), id=f"answer:{question.id}")

Ensure mirrors create_once / create_once_from; its links are applied only when the artifact is actually created.

For mutations, return Edit, Drop or Relate instead of calling effects:

from reactifact import Drop, Edit, Relate

return Edit(ticket, status="closed")          # effects.update
return Drop(ticket)                            # effects.delete
return Relate(answer, "supported_by", evidence)

Use effects for batch/conditional writes, or when the target id is computed at runtime. Returning None means "no changes" (a guard or a branch that did not apply).

docs.title: Idempotency sugar: create_once and upsert
docs.text:
A re-derived id (f"answer:{qid}") needs a guard — create_once folds it into the call itself:

handle = effects.create_once(Answer(...), id=f"answer:{qid}")
if handle is None:
    return None  # already answered — nothing to do

Create on an existing id is create-or-refresh (a new version of the same logical entity, §42/§43); upsert is the explicit name for that:

effects.upsert(Summary(...), id=f"summary:{doc_id}")

docs.title: Human and outbox are not effects
docs.text:
Effects is the data-write surface. Two non-data collaborators are injected next to it:

  • Human.ask(...) / Human.resume(...) — HITL, backed by PendingQuestion;
  • Outbox.act(...) — outbound side-effect intent, backed by PendingAction.
@step(produces=PendingAction, consumes=Ticket)
def notify(ticket: Ticket, outbox: Outbox) -> None:
    outbox.act("notify", key=f"notify:{ticket.id}", payload={"to": ticket.email})

Outbox.act creates a PendingAction under the stable id action:{key} (a retry or a branch that reaches the same action produces no second one). The step must not do the I/O; pass Runtime(dispatcher=...) and the runtime calls it once per committed intent, recording dispatched/failed. See patterns — Outbox and durability. Effects.ask/resume/act were removed; use Human/Outbox.

docs.title: Progress is neither data nor an effect
docs.text:
progress: Progress is the third injected collaborator — an ephemeral UI signal:

@step(produces=Answer, consumes=Question)
async def answer(question: Question, progress: Progress, llm: LLMProvider | None) -> Answer:
    progress("Считаю…", count=3)
    ...

It is a thin view over Context.announce, so it publishes a ProgressEvent immediately and never enters the commit. A step that only announces and then calls an LLM or tools does not need Context at all. When the status must survive a replay or appear in the run's receipt, model it as a status artifact (recipes.status.StatusMachine) instead.

docs.title: The three-layer picture
docs.text:
Layer What it is Who writes it Step the reaction: guard → LLM/calc → effects.* or a return value the application (you) Effects the stated change-set (creates/updates/links/questions), scoped to the run you, through the injected effects Patch the compiled operations the runtime applies as one commit the runtime

A side-effect-only step declares produces = () (or @step(produces=())) and optionally deletes = (T,); contracts then show no creates and the real delete targets. It still uses effects.delete/Drop like any other step.

Nothing is applied until the step returns — atomicity is structural (§41), no rollback machinery. Events, validation against produces, and trace reads/writes/relations all derive from the same compiled ops.

docs.title: Why effects are injected
docs.text: The effects slot is step-scoped: the runtime pushes a fresh one before each execution and pops it after (a contextvar) — safe under parallel steps. A class step names it as a parameter (effects: Effects); a function step reaches it through call.effects. You can build handles across statements (evidence created above is linked below), which is why call sites read "about artifacts", not "about ids".

docs.title: Where Patch still shows up
docs.text:
• StepGroup.run — the escape hatch for custom agents that assemble a change-set by hand.
  • Recipes (fan_out_sources, materialize_doc) write into the slot; return-style steps such as StatusMachine return an Edit instead. The tool loop (ToolUse/ToolUseHITL) and HITL (human.ask) are interaction, not direct data writes.
  • Tests and advanced assembly may still build a Patch; ordinary steps should not need it.

docs.title: The rule of thumb
docs.text:
guard → decide → describe (effects) → return None

If you find yourself writing Patch() inside a step — stop and write effects; the runtime does the compiling.

docs.title: The function form (@step) — same authoring surface
docs.text:
A decorated function receives call and uses call.effects:

from reactifact import StepCall, step

@step(produces=Answer, consumes=Question)
async def answer_turn(call: StepCall) -> None:
    question = call.trigger
    answer = call.effects.create(
        Answer(text=...), id=f"answer:{question.id}"
    )
    answer.link("derived_from", question)

Returning a model / list of models / Patch / None is compiled by the runtime, so short steps stay one-liners: def f(call): return Answer(...).

docs.title: Provenance is a query
docs.text:
Hand-written link calls are the explicit form. Two shortcuts keep the common case short without hiding the edges:

from reactifact import CALCULATED_FROM

@step(produces=Variance, consumes=Spend, provenance=CALCULATED_FROM)
def compute_variance(spend: Spend) -> Variance:
    return Variance(actual=spend.total, ...)

provenance= links every artifact the step actually resolved (not the whole consumes working set) to each artifact it creates. Import the names from reactifact (DERIVED_FROM, SUPPORTED_BY, CALCULATED_FROM, …) instead of spelling strings; a step whose produces is inferred from its return annotation gets DERIVED_FROM by default. An explicit link between the same pair wins, so the shortcut never overrides deliberate provenance.

Reading provenance is a query too:

context.sources(answer)            # ['transactions.csv', 'budget.csv', 'policy.md']
for link in context.why(answer):   # breadth-first over outgoing edges
    print("  " * link.depth, link.relation, type(link.artifact.data).__name__)

why() follows supported_by / calculated_from / … edges breadth-first; pass relations=(...) to restrict the walk and max_depth= to stop it. Use SUPPORTED_BY only for answers/claims; compute steps are CALCULATED_FROM or DERIVED_FROM.

docs.title: Which style to reach for
docs.text: The subclass and @step function are the two canonical styles — pick subclass when the step has logic worth naming as a class, @step for a short one-off. Overriding StepGroup.run(self, event, context) -> Patch remains a low-level escape hatch, not an everyday authoring style.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
The deterministic metrics and experiment layer are rendered in the evaluation API reference. harness (§56)

Because state is structured, evaluation is multi-level — not just answer == expected:

Evidence quality · Claim verification · Confidence calibration · Provenance grounding · Calculation correctness · Answer coverage · Source coverage

reactifact.eval is the deterministic, LLM-free harness that scores a run's final state. Each metric is a pure function over the resulting Context (+ optional ground truth), so truthfulness is measured where it lives — the artifact graph — not the smoothness of the text.

docs.title: Running a suite
docs.text:
from reactifact.eval import EvalCase, calculation_correctness, core_metrics, run_suite

cases = [
    EvalCase(
        name="calc-question",
        run=_run_knowledge_calc,               # executes the pipeline → Context
        expected={"sources": ["costs:", "pricing:", "guide:"]},
    ),
]
report = run_suite(cases, metrics={
    **core_metrics,                          # answer/provenance/evidence/claim
    "calc": calculation_correctness(values=(5480, 3580)),
    "sources": source_coverage(),
})
print(report.render())

eval · multi-level report (§56)

[calc-question] overall 1.000
    answer_present            1.000
    provenance_grounded       1.000
    evidence_quality          1.000
    claim_verification        1.000
    calc                      1.000
    sources                   1.000

suite overall: 1.000

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Artifact classes are matched by name (Answer, Evidence, …), so the harness needs no domain imports — the domain stays out of the framework.

Metric What it answers Built-in answer_present did the run produce an answer at all? plain fn provenance_grounded is every answer backed by an existing supported_by (§34)? plain fn evidence_quality(threshold=0.5) share of evidence scoring at/above the bar plain fn claim_verification(valid=("verified",)) share of claims that passed verification (§35) plain fn confidence_calibration() Brier score of Claim.confidence against actual correctness (§56) factory (needs expected.claim_correctness) answer_coverage() coverage of the expected answer text by the answer factory (needs expected.answer) calculation_correctness(values=…) share of calculations matching ground truth (§67) factory source_coverage() share of the answer's sources matched by markers factory (needs expected.sources)

core_metrics bundles the four non-generative ones. A metric that lacks ground truth returns None and is reported as skipped (EvalResult.skipped), never as a silent zero.

docs.title: Retrieval metrics
docs.text:
Retrieval is scored before an answer exists. reactifact.eval.retrieval is knowledge-agnostic: it scores ranked identifiers against ground truth, and a key callable maps whatever the retriever returns to that identifier.

from reactifact.eval import RetrievalCase, evaluate_retrieval

report = await evaluate_retrieval(
    [RetrievalCase("install", relevant=["install.md"])],
    retrieve=lambda query, limit: pipeline.query(query, top_k=limit),
    k=5,
    key=lambda hit: hit.source_uri,
)
print(report.render())   # recall, precision, mrr, ndcg, hit_rate

relevant may be a list (binary) or a mapping {id: gain} for graded nDCG. Duplicate ids are collapsed, and a case without relevant ids is skipped. reactifact.knowledge.eval.evaluate_pipeline is the ready-made adapter with document_key/chunk_key.

docs.title: Dataset evaluation
docs.text:
Beyond scoring one already-built Context, reactifact.eval runs a dataset through a target and scores every example — the offline-evaluation loop, with no hosted store:

from reactifact.eval import (
    Dataset, evaluate, from_metric, judge_correctness, summary_pass_rate,
)

dataset = Dataset.from_file("evals/qa.json")       # or from_list / .jsonl
report = evaluate(
    dataset,
    target=lambda inputs: my_pipeline(**inputs),   # Context | ScenarioResult | {outputs} | RunResult
    evaluators={
        "present": from_metric("answer_present", answer_present),
        "coverage": from_metric("coverage", answer_coverage()),
        "correctness": judge_correctness(llm),      # P2: LLM-as-judge
    },
    summary=[summary_pass_rate(0.8)],
)
report.assert_passed({"correctness": 0.7})          # CI gate (raises EvalFailure)

Example carries inputs (fed to the target), optional reference_outputs (used only by evaluators) and metadata; its id is content-derived, so Dataset.version pins a run to a dataset revision. A target may return a Context, a ScenarioResult from reactifact.testing (read via .context/ .trace), a plain outputs mapping, or a RunResult. evaluate runs examples sequentially in dataset order (max_concurrency=N parallelizes I/O-bound targets). Pass on_result=callback to receive each EvalResult as soon as it is scored — a progress hook for long suites; with max_concurrency > 0 the callbacks fire in completion order. The returned EvalReport is unchanged.

report = evaluate(
    dataset,
    target=my_pipeline,
    evaluators=evaluators,
    on_result=lambda result: print(f"{result.case}: {result.overall():.2f}"),
)

docs.title: Experiments / Arena
docs.text:
reactifact.experiments.Experiment runs several variants over the same dataset, scores each with the evaluators above, and picks a winner by quality (cost and latency break ties):

from reactifact.experiments import Experiment

result = await Experiment(
    base=context,
    variants={"gpt": gpt_agents, "claude": claude_agents},
    dataset=Dataset.from_file("evals/qa.json"),
    seed=lambda ctx, inputs: ctx.create(Question(text=inputs["question"])),
    evaluators=[exact_answer],
    metric="exact_answer",       # sequence evaluators are keyed by __name__
).run()

print(result.render())           # markdown table + winner
winner_contexts = result.winner_result.contexts

Each example runs on its own base.branch(), so variants never mutate the base or each other; VariantResult carries the EvalReport, per-run RunStats (cost/tokens/latency) and the contexts. The returned contexts are real branches — inspect them, or merge a chosen one yourself.

docs.title: Evaluators
docs.text:
An Evaluator is any callable EvalInput -> Feedback | bool | float | {key: score} | list | None; None skips (no ground truth / not applicable — never a silent zero). EvalInput exposes the example, the extracted outputs, and — for reactifact runs — the final context and trace. from_metric wraps any scoring metric into an evaluator:

evaluators = {
    "grounded": from_metric("provenance_grounded", provenance_grounded),
    "calc": from_metric("calc", calculation_correctness(values=(5480, 3580))),
}

trajectory_match(mode, steps=…) compares the path a run took against example.reference_outputs["trajectory"] — the typed-graph analogue of message-trajectory matching. steps is "agents" (the agent path), "events", "reads"/"writes" ("create:Answer", …) or a custom EvalInput -> list[str]:

Mode Meaning strict same steps, same order unordered same multiset of steps subset actual ⊆ expected (no unexpected steps) superset expected ⊆ actual (at least the required steps)

docs.title: LLM-as-judge
docs.text:
For subjective quality there is no deterministic metric; an LLM grades the output against a rubric. llm_judge turns any LLMProvider into an Evaluator, so a judge is just another model call — it composes with CachingLLM/budget/metrics and is faked in tests with FakeLLM:

from reactifact.eval import judge_correctness, judge_faithfulness, judge_relevance

judge_correctness(llm, continuous=True, choices=[0.0, 0.5, 1.0])   # reference-based
judge_relevance(llm)        # reference-free: does it answer the question?
judge_faithfulness(llm)     # reference-free: grounded in the context?

The judge is asked for strict JSON ({"score": …, "comment": …}); parsing is tolerant (scans for the first JSON object, then a number/boolean). continuous yields a 0..1 float; choices snaps to a fixed scale; include_reference formats the reference outputs into the prompt (reference-based grading).

docs.title: Gate & summary
docs.text: EvalReport.aggregate() is the mean per metric key; passed(…) / assert_passed(…) (or module-level assert_eval) is the CI gate — a threshold for a key no case measured is not met. Summary evaluators (summary_pass_rate(threshold), summary_mean(key)) aggregate across the whole suite into EvalReport.summary.

docs.title: Online evaluation
docs.text:
The same evaluators can score live runs instead of a curated dataset: reactifact.eval.online samples finished runs from a TraceStore, scores them, and writes the verdicts back as tags (the reviewer-annotation channel the dashboard already reads) plus metrics.

from reactifact.eval import (
    OnlineEvalConfig, OnlineEvaluator, judge_relevance, output_present,
)
from reactifact.tracing import TraceStore

store = TraceStore("traces.db")
evaluator = OnlineEvaluator(
    store,
    OnlineEvalConfig(
        evaluators={"present": output_present(), "relevance": judge_relevance(llm)},
        sample_rate=0.1,            # score 10% of matching runs
        tag="eval", failure_tag="eval:failed",
    ),
    metrics=metrics,                # any reactifact.metrics.Metrics
)
await evaluator.run_once()          # one batch
# or, in a FastAPI lifespan task:
await evaluator.run_forever(interval_seconds=300)

A trace is a summary — artifact data and LLM messages are truncated for storage — so a source decides what is scoreable:

  • trace_source() (default): scores the RunTrace itself — the run's typed path (trajectory_match), and output_present/no_errors over the outputs and spans. A metric that needs data the trace no longer carries is skipped.
  • context_source(run_fn): the app rebuilds the full Context for a run id, so core_metrics, from_metric(...) and judges see complete data.
  • OnlineEvalConfig.reference_fn(run) supplies per-run ground truth (e.g. an expected trajectory) when scoring a reference-based metric.

sample_rate/strategy/seed choose which runs (reproducible under a seed); on_report observes each batch. FastAPI apps can mount create_online_eval_router(evaluator) — POST /api/evals/run, GET /api/evals/report, GET /api/evals/summary — and the CLI scores a store in one command:

reactifact eval traces.db --sample 1.0
reactifact eval traces.db --evaluators judge --provider openai:gpt-4o-mini
reactifact check my_app.pipeline:pipeline --evals evals/qa.json --overall 0.8

reactifact check is the dataset gate: it runs the pipeline over a Dataset with the core metrics and exits non-zero when --overall/--gate is not met.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
• Metric — one measured 0..1 score with a reporting weight.
  • EvalCase — name + a run() -> Context + optional expected ground truth.
  • EvalResult (per case) / EvalReport (suite) — overall() (weighted mean), aggregate(), passed(), to_dict(), render().
  • Example / Dataset — versioned evaluation examples + JSON/JSONL loading.
  • EvalInput / Feedback / Evaluator — an evaluator's inputs and verdict.
  • RunResult — a normalized target result (outputs + optional context/trace).
  • EvalFailure — raised by the gate (AssertionError subclass).

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text: tests/test_eval.py scores the knowledge calculation question offline (no LLM); tests/test_eval_dataset.py, test_eval_trajectory.py and test_eval_judge.py cover the dataset loop, trajectory matching and the judge (a FakeLLM returning JSON).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Thirteen runnable examples ship in examples/ (in-repo, not packaged). Twelve are full applications; tour isolates the primitives. They are the reference implementations for the recipes, patterns and the port matrix — canonical examples are split into a steps/ package (stages) plus thin web.py/chat.py/main.py entries.

All demos run with or without API keys: configure .env (copy .env.example) for LLM/embedder/image providers, or let them fall back to deterministic demo mode.

The session-chat demos (knowledge, devops, repair) build their web layer on the canonical reactifact.chat + reactifact.web contract — each supplies only the domain hooks (agents, input model, terminal reply), and the SSE transport and session persistence come from the framework.

docs.title: What each example teaches
docs.text:
Example What it teaches Shape starter_app minimal FastAPI app over the quick cases on-ramp; no auth/settings knowledge multi-source RAG, evidence and deterministic CSV calculation domain web app knowledge_base connector → chunks → index, incremental state, hybrid query ingestion/CLI medic_lab competing hypotheses, scoring, HITL steering domain service devops HITL tools, authz, per-user memory, traces closest to production; demo auth code_review deterministic diff rules + optional LLM, linked report CLI/worker repair stage-driven replanning, budget, HITL domain web app chat minimal transcript + bounded ChatMemory offline chat forklab branch/merge, conflicts and policies CLI/state exploration fintech_audit computed, reproducible answer with context hash CLI/auditable pipeline outbox committed side effects, retry and replay worker/daemon pattern repo_agent destructive tool behind approval CLI/guardrail tour framework primitives in small scenes learning

Use this table to pick the example closest to your problem. If you read only three, start with starter_app (smallest web), devops (tools/authz/memory) and fintech_audit (computed, reproducible answer). Examples stay deliberately focused; they do not all carry auth/settings. The production-shaped scaffold is reactifact new app|daemon, not another example.

docs.title: starter_app — a copy-pasteable web app over the quick cases
docs.text:
What it shows: one FastAPI process you can clone and run, covering the shapes most apps start with — a structured call, RAG with citations, an LLM with tools, and a session-persisted chat — plus a trace dashboard for all of them. It's a thin skin over reactifact.quick, and the provider is chosen by from_env(): no key → offline/deterministic fallbacks (RAG still answers from knowledge/ with citations); OPENROUTER_API_KEY → OpenRouter; OPENAI_BASE_URL → any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Copy the directory and swap the domain.

uv sync --extra web
uv run python -m examples.starter_app.app      # http://127.0.0.1:8000

docs.title: knowledge — multi-source chat with evidence
docs.text:
What it shows: fan_out_sources over a reactifact.knowledge index + a structured CSV source → lazy materialize_doc → evidence extraction → claim verification → answer with provenance; deterministic CSV calculation (Spreadsheet → Calculation). The web app also mounts /traces (agent runs with Question/Answer columns), /contracts (static consumes/produces/tools) and /knowledge/ (ingestion status).

uv run python ./examples/knowledge/web.py    # FastAPI/SSE + trace dashboard
uv run python ./examples/knowledge/chat.py   # interactive CLI
uv run python -m examples.knowledge.eval    # offline retrieval metrics

Key files: steps/ (common, router, search, evidence, calc, lifecycle), step_groups.py, web.py.

docs.title: knowledge_base — code-first ingestion and retrieval
docs.text:
What it shows: the optional reactifact.knowledge layer over a real corpus: Connector -> RawDocument -> Document -> Chunk -> EmbeddingProvider -> Index, incremental DocStore state, and hybrid (BM25 + RRF) retrieval. Defaults to SQLite and a deterministic embedder, so it runs offline; --qdrant-url switches the index without changing the pipeline.

uv run python examples/knowledge_base/build.py --docs docs/en --query "sources"
uv run python examples/knowledge_base/build.py --docs docs/en --store sqlite
uv run python examples/knowledge_base/build.py --docs docs/en --qdrant-url http://localhost:6333

Key files: build.py (connector, pipeline wiring, query). See Knowledge base.

docs.title: medic_lab — hypothesis laboratory
docs.text:
What it shows: one question spawns competing hypotheses; each is investigated over an evidence pool; scored by support/contradiction counts (scores are calculated, not guessed); HITL steering via PendingQuestion; honest report when evidence is insufficient; concurrency_limit (LLM agents = 2, global cap = 6).

uv run python ./examples/medic_lab/main.py    # serves uvicorn automatically

docs.title: devops — HITL tool agent (ops assistant)
docs.text:
What it shows: HITLLMAgent + LLM tool router (routing is a separate structured step, StructuredLLM), HITL-approved mutations for Kubernetes, GitLab, Ansible (each is a fateful operation the LLM cannot dream up on its own); trace dashboard with the create_trace_router UI and a /contracts page. It also carries the trust & safety layer: guardrails.py defines a custom guardrail (a destructive production change must cite a CHG- ticket) plus secret redaction, wired onto RuntimeResources in one line — the ops policy blocks injection and unapproved prod changes, redacts PII/secrets, and screens the raw input too. And it scores its own traffic: online_eval.py samples served runs from the trace store (trace_source, custom routed/routed_to evaluators), tags passes eval / failures eval:failed, and web.py mounts create_online_eval_router (POST /api/evals/run). Two demo identities show the multi-user layer: admin1 (admin) and admin2 (analyst), picked in the UI and sent as X-User (demo authentication only). Each runs with a Principal + PermissionPolicy (policy.py), so admin2 can chat, use k8s and GitLab but is refused before the Ansible agent starts. Long-term memory is per-user (MemoryStore(namespace="user:<name>")): a report summary is recorded as an outbox PendingAction (remember_after_commit) and indexed after the report commits (MemoryStore.dispatch), so a failed turn cannot leave a dangling entry; recall is folded into routing in later sessions, never copied from the chat history, and never visible in the other user's namespace. Run the standalone demos (no LLM, no network):

uv run python ./examples/devops/web.py      # SSE UI + trace dashboard
uv run python ./examples/devops/safety.py   # custom guardrails, end to end
uv run python ./examples/devops/online_eval.py   # online-eval over served runs

docs.title: code_review — deterministic-first review agent
docs.text:
What it shows: a unified diff → ChangedFile → per-file FileReview (deterministic rules plus an optional LLM) → ReviewReport with Markdown findings. Rules catch eval/exec, shell=True, hardcoded secrets, bare except, TODO and debug print; the report links back to every reviewed file (reviewed relation). Runs offline with no API key.

python -m examples.code_review.main --demo
git diff | python -m examples.code_review.main

docs.title: repair — budget-aware replanning (Russian by design)
docs.text:
What it shows: chat and catalog data are intentionally Russian — the contrast with other English examples is deliberate (localization is a product concern, not a framework one). The flow: fact collection → LLM design options → 3 photo previews → plan → deterministic catalog estimate → HITL approval → budget complaint triggers a rebuild from an earlier stage with a _downstream_resets rollback. Everything explicit is deterministic; only genuinely generative steps use the LLM.

The web app mounts /traces and /contracts next to the chat.

uv run python ./examples/repair/web.py
uv run python ./examples/repair/chat.py

docs.title: chat — minimal single-model multi-turn conversation (offline)
docs.text:
What it shows: the simple multi-turn shape in ~80 lines — one message model (ConversationMessage) both sides write. Conversation records turns (create_turn) and renders the thread (transcript/state); ChatMemory with keep= bounds it (WindowPruner) — wired through Chat. No LLM, no API key (a deterministic echo agent answers). The heterogeneous shape (separate question/answer types) is in the repair/devops/knowledge examples, via Transcript/MessageSpec — see Multi-turn & chat.

.venv/bin/python -m examples.chat.main

docs.title: forklab — branch & merge (§39-§40)
docs.text:
What it shows: deterministic alternative-state exploration — one question, two research strategies on their own forks (Context.branch()); a three-way merge() that either unions cleanly or raises an explicit MergeConflict (§40, never a silent choice); an evaluator over the merged state whose Answer is linked supported_by to findings from both branches. Fully offline (§67) — the point is the state semantics, not a model. A --conflict flag demonstrates the conflict-and-policy-resolve loop.

uv run python -m examples.forklab.main            # happy path
uv run python -m examples.forklab.main --mermaid  # merged provenance graph
uv run python -m examples.forklab.main --conflict # explicit MergeConflict + policy

The same pattern is the natural base for rewriting medic_lab: hypotheses become real forks instead of tag-routed channels.

docs.title: fintech_audit — auditable, reproducible answer
docs.text:
What it shows: a finance question ("what is the Q2 cloud spend variance, and does policy require approval?") answered from a transactions CSV, a budget CSV and a policy document. The audit story, end to end: the figures are computed in plain Python (the model is never the source of truth, §67); every derived artifact links to what it came from; reactifact.audit.build_report renders the answer with a content hash per artifact and a context_sha256 for the run; and re-running the pipeline hashes identically — the check reactifact replay <store> --session <id> --verify <hash> runs against a saved session. Offline, no key.

uv run python -m examples.fintech_audit.main

See also reactifact/audit.py (build_report, context_hash, report_to_markdown) and Observability for shipping such a run to a sink with redactor=.

docs.title: outbox — external effects as committed state
docs.text:
What it shows: the outbox contract in seven deterministic cases — a step records outbox.act(...) instead of doing I/O; Runtime(dispatcher=...) sends after the commit; re-derivation, same-generation duplicates, merged branches, replay, failure→retry and an app-owned retry wrapper all keep one delivery. No LLM, no network; the fake dispatcher makes the count visible.

uv run python -m examples.outbox.main

See Outbox in production for the at-least-once contract and the app-owned drain/retry policy.

docs.title: repo_agent — a destructive tool behind approval
docs.text:
What it shows: a HITLLMAgent coding assistant over a tiny repository. read_file and run_tests run immediately; git_commit is @tool(destructive=True), so the runtime turns the model's decision into a PendingQuestion(kind="approve") and executes only after context.resume(...). The provider is scripted, so the demo is offline and deterministic.

uv run python -m examples.repo_agent.main

docs.title: tour — the framework primitives in seventeen small scenes
docs.text:
What it shows: the parts that are easy to miss when reading a full app: typed artifacts with version_history / diff / compact; typed inputs with Latest, implicit read-only inputs and Consume(..., debounce=True); a SQLite session that survives a restart, resumes a pending event and replays an earlier commit; an optional LLM step; agent retries and per-step deadlines; a schema-backed HITL question resumed with a Pydantic model; checkpoints/forks; the typed Runtime.astream_events modes; an optimistic-write conflict resolved by a merge policy; and a subflow on an isolated Context with a parent-run trace link, plus a MapReduce fan-out/reduce, a peer-to-peer swarm handoff, tool record/replay via Runtime.replay_run, an A/B experiment with a winner, a static contract validation, namespaced long-term memory, and an offline knowledge pipeline with hybrid retrieval and metrics. Every scene is offline by default, and the model scene runs with a provider only when --llm is passed.

uv run python -m examples.tour.main                 # all scenes, offline
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene state   # versions + compaction
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene durable --db /tmp/tour.sqlite3
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene resilience
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene hitl
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene knowledge
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene time_travel
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene events
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene conflicts
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene subflow
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene map_reduce
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene swarm
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene replay
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene experiment
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene validate
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --scene memory
uv run python -m examples.tour.main --llm --scene model

With --llm, from_env() reads examples/tour/.env (copy .env.example); without a provider the model scene prints an honest deterministic brief. See examples/tour.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
.venv/bin/python -m pytest      # full suite (PostgreSQL cases skip without TEST_PG_DSN)
.venv/bin/mypy                  # strict typing across the repo
.venv/bin/ruff check            # lint

uv sync installs the dev+web groups from pyproject.toml; uv build ships only the reactifact wheel (examples and docs are not packaged).

docs.title: Knowledge base
docs.text:
Every class and function on this page is rendered from its docstring in the knowledge API reference. (optional layer)

reactifact.knowledge turns heterogeneous documents into a searchable index without adding a second agent framework. It is code-first: a connector is an object, configuration is ordinary Python, and there is no YAML loader, CLI, plugin registry or type-string factory.

The layer is intentionally separate from the reactive core. reactifact never imports it; it imports core protocols and reuses the embedder already wired into RuntimeResources:

Connector -> RawDocument -> Document -> Chunk -> EmbeddingProvider -> Index

Install-time it is just the core package (pip install "reactifact[knowledge]"); the extra adds no runtime dependencies. The bundled examples/knowledge demo uses this layer for its text corpus.

docs.title: Source vs Connector
docs.text:
Two capabilities, two lifecycles:

Source (reactifact.sources) Connector (reactifact.knowledge) When query time, inside an agent ingestion time, before queries Does search(query) + resolve(ref) fetch() / list_documents() Returns SourceRef RawDocument Example CSVSource, WebSource FilesystemConnector, your API connector

IndexSource is the bridge: it turns an already-built knowledge index into a regular Source for RuntimeResources.sources.

docs.title: Build a pipeline
docs.text:
from reactifact import RuntimeResources
from reactifact.knowledge import (
    KnowledgePipeline,
    ProviderEmbedder,
    SectionsChunker,
    SqliteIndex,
)
from reactifact.providers import embedder_from_env

resources = RuntimeResources(embedder=embedder_from_env())

pipeline = KnowledgePipeline(
    connector,
    chunker=SectionsChunker(max_tokens=400, overlap=60),
    embedder=ProviderEmbedder(resources.embedder),  # core provider
    index=SqliteIndex(".reactifact/knowledge.db"),
)

report = await pipeline.run(
    incremental=True,
    state_path=".reactifact/knowledge/state.json",
)

connector is any object with a source_id and an async fetch() returning RawDocuments. Add list_documents() and fetch(uris=...) to make incremental runs skip downloading unchanged bodies:

from reactifact.knowledge import DocumentMeta, RawDocument

class DocsConnector:
    source_id = "docs"

    async def list_documents(self) -> list[DocumentMeta]:
        ...

    async def fetch(self, *, uris: set[str] | None = None) -> list[RawDocument]:
        ...

RawDocument.from_text(...) is the common code-first helper. Metadata (documentId, sourceUrl, title) is merged into every chunk, so citations survive retrieval. Built-in chunkers also add section_index, chunk_index and heading coordinates, which is enough to render and highlight a citation.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
hits = await pipeline.query(
    "how do I install it?",
    top_k=5,
    hybrid=True,          # dense + BM25, fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion
    filters={"space": "ENG"},
    principals=["alice"], # optional ACL check
)
for hit in hits:
    print(hit.source_uri, hit.score, hit.text[:80])

Retrieval is scoped to the pipeline's source_id; in a shared index, another source's chunks never leak into the result. Pass source_id= to query a different source explicitly, or pass a bare index plus embedder= to reactifact.knowledge.query(...).

min_score filters dense cosine results only. Hybrid scores are rank-fusion scores, not similarities, so min_score with hybrid=True raises ConfigError instead of silently dropping results. hybrid=True also requires an index with keyword_search; dense-only indexes must use hybrid=False.

max_per_document=N keeps at most N chunks of the same document in the result, so one long document cannot crowd out everything else. Documents are identified by document_id/documentId metadata, falling back to source_uri. The cap is applied before rerank, so the reranker sees a diverse candidate set.

mmr=MMR(lambda_=0.3) re-ranks over-fetched candidates by relevance and novelty (Maximal Marginal Relevance). lambda_=1 is pure relevance, 0 is pure novelty; the pipeline embeds candidate texts with its own embedder, after min_score/max_per_document and before rerank. query_by_vector requires embedder= when MMR is used.

Every hit carries retrieval provenance: dense_rank, keyword_rank, rerank_rank, score_kind ("dense" or "rrf") and a stable chunk_id. IndexSource puts them under SourceRef.metadata["retrieval"] and uses the chunk id as the ref fragment, so two chunks of one document get distinct artifact ids.

Already have a vector? query_by_vector(...) runs the same retrieval without embedding the text. Pass query_text= when using hybrid=True (BM25 needs the words) or rerank= (the reranker needs the query).

docs.title: Retrieval metrics
docs.text:
reactifact.eval.retrieval scores ranking quality without an answer: recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG@k and hit rate. reactifact.knowledge.eval wires a pipeline to those metrics:

from reactifact.eval import RetrievalCase
from reactifact.knowledge import evaluate_pipeline

report = await evaluate_pipeline(
    pipeline,
    [
        RetrievalCase("how do I install?", relevant=["install.md"]),
        RetrievalCase("refund policy", relevant={"refund.md": 2.0}),
    ],
    k=5,
    hybrid=True,
)
print(report.render())
report.assert_passed({"recall": 0.9})   # CI gate

relevant is a list (binary) or a mapping (graded gains). The default key compares documents (documentId, falling back to source_uri); pass key=chunk_key for chunk-level metrics. cases_from_dataset(dataset) builds cases from inputs["query"] and reference_outputs["relevant"]. A case without relevant ids is skipped, never scored as zero.

docs.title: Rerank
docs.text:
The base hook is domain code: relevance policy is yours. query exposes it, and an optional LLM-backed helper is available below:

from collections.abc import Sequence
from reactifact.knowledge import SearchHit

def prefer_runbooks(
    query: str, hits: Sequence[SearchHit], top_k: int
) -> list[SearchHit]:
    ranked = sorted(
        hits,
        key=lambda hit: hit.metadata.get("kind") != "runbook",
    )
    return [hit.model_copy(update={"score": 1.0 - i / len(ranked)})
            for i, hit in enumerate(ranked[:top_k])]

hits = await pipeline.query(
    "checkout is timing out",
    top_k=5,
    hybrid=True,
    rerank=prefer_runbooks,
)
  • Called after dense/hybrid retrieval and min_score, before the final top_k cut.
  • Receives over-fetched candidates (top_k * 4), so it has room to promote or filter.
  • May be synchronous or asynchronous; return any subset in any order.
  • Exceptions propagate. This is application code, and silently falling back to the original order would hide relevance bugs. For best-effort retrieval, wrap it:
async def safe_rerank(query, hits, top_k):
    try:
        return await my_reranker(query, hits, top_k)
    except Exception:
        logger.warning("domain rerank failed", exc_info=True)
        return list(hits[:top_k])

docs.title: Ready-made LLM reranker
docs.text:
llm_reranker is an opt-in factory, not a separate client: it uses the core chat LLMProvider, which is independent of the embedding provider used to build the index.

from reactifact.knowledge import llm_reranker

rerank = llm_reranker(
    resources.llm,  # chat provider, not resources.embedder
    instructions="Prefer runbooks; ignore deprecated docs.",
)
hits = await pipeline.query("checkout is timing out", top_k=5, rerank=rerank)

A domain prompt can replace both levels:

from reactifact.knowledge import RERANK_OUTPUT_CONTRACT, llm_reranker

def render(query, hits, top_k):
    lines = [f"Query: {query}"]
    for index, hit in enumerate(hits, start=1):
        kind = hit.metadata.get("kind", "doc")
        lines.append(f"[{index}] ({kind}) {hit.text[:800]}")
    return "\n".join(lines)

rerank = llm_reranker(
    resources.llm,
    system_prompt=(
        "You rank NikaRD support excerpts. "
        + RERANK_OUTPUT_CONTRACT
        + " Prefer runbooks over marketing pages; prefer newer docs on ties."
    ),
    user_prompt=render,
)
  • system_prompt replaces the default system prompt — keep RERANK_OUTPUT_CONTRACT in it.
  • instructions appends domain rules to the default prompt.
  • user_prompt replaces the numbered-excerpt renderer and receives full SearchHit objects, so it can use metadata (kind, documentId, ...).
  • Fails soft: a provider error, invalid JSON or a non-permutation response calls on_error (or logs a warning) and keeps the original order. The raw rerank= hook stays fail-loud.
  • Hybrid retrieval first: an LLM rerank adds latency, cost and non-determinism.

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text:
Index Persistence Notes MemoryIndex process tests, small prototypes; supports keyword search SqliteIndex one file zero infrastructure, brute-force cosine; supports keyword search QdrantIndex remote raw REST client (no SDK); collection created on demand; hybrid narrows server-side then BM25-ranks locally PgVectorIndex Postgres pg extra; requires CREATE EXTENSION vector; cosine; server-side metadata/ACL filters and tsvector keyword search ChromaIndex local dir / remote client optional chromadb extra; cosine distance; dense only (hybrid=True raises ConfigError); pass client= to reuse an existing Chroma client

All backends implement deterministic point IDs, per-source reconcile, metadata filters and optional ACL visibility. Point IDs include the chunker's chunk_index, so identical bodies in two sections stay distinct. Switching backends does not change the pipeline.

Built-in indexes validate vector dimensionality: the first upsert pins the size, and a later vector of a different size raises ConfigError before anything is written. A changed embedding model therefore fails at the boundary instead of deep inside a database client. ChromaIndex additionally relies on Chroma's own collection check for existing data.

Optional capabilities are runtime-checkable protocols, not getattr probes: KeywordIndexer (keyword_search), BatchIndexer (upsert_batch) and CountableIndex (count). An adapter implements only what it supports; the pipeline checks the protocol and uses the capability or raises a clear ConfigError.

PgVectorIndex requires pip install "reactifact[pg]" and a database with the pgvector extension. Pass dsn= or dsn_env=; text_search_config defaults to simple (language-neutral) and can be english for stemming. ChromaIndex is optional: pip install "reactifact[knowledge-chroma]". Metadata values are stringified for Chroma's scalar-only metadata; the full original metadata is preserved under __metadata and returned in SearchHit.metadata.

docs.title: Incremental ingestion
docs.text:
run(incremental=True) keeps DocStore state keyed by source identity and a pipeline signature (extraction, chunking, embedding settings). Changing chunk size or the embedding model invalidates fingerprints instead of leaving stale chunks. The document hash covers content type and metadata as well as bytes, so an ACL/title/tag change re-indexes even when the text is unchanged. State is committed only after a successful run. Runs are serialized per (state_path, source_id) within the process; across processes the contract is one ingestion writer per source (use an external lock if you fan out).

A connector failure aborts before reconciliation, so a transient outage never makes the corpus look deleted.

docs.title: DocStore backends
docs.text:
DocStore is a protocol. JsonDocStore (the default behind state_path=) is one JSON file rewritten on save — fine for small corpora. SqliteDocStore keeps the same fingerprints and run ledger in SQLite with transactional per-row writes:

from reactifact.knowledge import SqliteDocStore

docstore = SqliteDocStore(".reactifact/knowledge/state.sqlite3")
await pipeline.run(docstore=docstore)

Both expose entry/commit/save/record_run/runs/snapshot, so the pipeline and the status router do not care which backend is used. Pass docstore= explicitly to choose SQLite; state_path= keeps using JSON.

docs.title: Failure isolation, progress and concurrency
docs.text:
By default a bad document aborts the run (on_error="fail_fast"). For large corpora, collect failures and keep going:

from reactifact.knowledge import IngestProgress

events: list[IngestProgress] = []
report = await pipeline.run(
    incremental=True,
    on_error="collect",
    on_progress=events.append,
)
report.documents_failed       # count
report.failures               # [IngestFailure(uri, stage, error), ...]

A failed document is not committed to DocStore; its previous index points are kept and the next incremental run retries it. on_progress receives stage events (start, fetch, extract, embed, index, reconcile, done) plus per-document/failed events with counts.

document_concurrency (default 1) parallelizes extract/chunk across documents; progress events arrive as each document finishes. Connector fetching remains owned by the connector; ProviderEmbedder already batches/concurrently embeds.

run(..., batch_size=N) bounds ingestion memory: with a ListingConnector only one batch of bodies is fetched, extracted, embedded and upserted at a time, and per-batch pending chunks/vectors are released. State is still committed once at the end; a fail-fast error leaves earlier batches indexed but unreconciled, so the next run repairs them.

Without a DocStore (non-incremental runs) a failed document has no previous hash to restore, so on_error="collect" skips deletion reconciliation for that run: successful documents are still upserted, but nothing is deleted. Use incremental=True for the full keep-and-retry behavior.

docs.title: Bridge to the agent runtime
docs.text:
The two integrations are explicit and optional:

from reactifact.knowledge import IndexSource, IngestStep

# retrieval as a regular reactifact Source
source = IndexSource(pipeline, hybrid=True)
ctx = Context(resources=RuntimeResources(embedder=..., sources={"kb": source}))

# ingestion as a step (when ingestion belongs to the reactive flow)
step = IngestStep(pipeline)  # returns an IngestReportArtifact

For most services ingestion is a background job, not an agent step: call pipeline.run(...) directly from the scheduler/worker and only expose IndexSource to agents.

IndexSource(expand="section") (or "document") makes resolve return the parent section/document instead of the matched chunk: it re-fetches the source document and runs the same extractor, so parent text is never stored in the index. Expansion uses per-URI fetch(uris=...) for ListingConnectors and a full fetch for plain connectors; a missing document or section raises KnowledgeError, which materialize_doc reports through on_error.

IndexSource(principals=["alice"]) (or a callable returning principals) applies ACL filtering to every search, so RAG cannot silently query without an identity. require_principals=True turns a missing identity into a ConfigError instead of an unfiltered search.

docs.title: Custom connectors and indexes
docs.text:
The built-in FilesystemConnector covers the common local-docs case:

from reactifact.knowledge import FilesystemConnector, KnowledgePipeline

pipeline = KnowledgePipeline(
    FilesystemConnector("docs", source_id="docs"),
    embedder=embedder,
    index=index,
)

It provides content fingerprints and fetch(uris=...), so incremental runs skip unchanged files. A missing root raises SourceError instead of treating the corpus as empty and reconciling it away.

docs.title: Built-in connectors and extractors
docs.text:
Connector Notes FilesystemConnector text files under a directory; content hashes; per-URI fetch HttpConnector explicit URLs or a sitemap; ETag/Last-Modified fingerprints; httpx is a core dependency S3Connector one bucket with an optional prefix; ETag listing; knowledge-s3 (boto3) Extractor Input Extra MarkdownExtractor Markdown / plain text — HtmlExtractor static HTML — CsvExtractor CSV → Markdown table sections — JsonExtractor JSON objects/arrays → sections — PdfExtractor one section per PDF page knowledge-pdf (pypdf) DocxExtractor DOCX headings, paragraphs, tables knowledge-office (python-docx)

AutoExtractor dispatches by content type, then by URI suffix. Optional extractors are imported lazily and the error names the extra to install.

from reactifact.knowledge import HttpConnector

pipeline = KnowledgePipeline(
    HttpConnector(sitemap="https://docs.example/sitemap.xml"),
    embedder=embedder,
    index=index,
)

There is no registry to extend — implement the protocol and pass an instance:

  • Source connectors satisfy Connector (source_id + fetch()), or ListingConnector (adds list_documents() and fetch(uris=...) for cheap incremental skips).
  • Vector stores satisfy Indexer (upsert, reconcile, search); add KeywordIndexer.keyword_search for hybrid retrieval, BatchIndexer.upsert_batch for bulk writes and CountableIndex.count for the status page. These are runtime-checkable protocols: implementing the method is the whole registration step.

MemoryIndex, SqliteIndex, QdrantIndex, PgVectorIndex and ChromaIndex are reference implementations of the same contract; a Milvus adapter is just another class passed as index=.

docs.title: Status page (optional FastAPI router)
docs.text:
Ingestion is a background job, not an agent run, so it does not go into RunTrace. The knowledge layer ships a separate read-only router that reads the DocStore run ledger:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from reactifact.knowledge.web import create_knowledge_router

app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(
    create_knowledge_router(docstore, index=pipeline.index),
    prefix="/knowledge",
)
  • GET /knowledge/ — per-source last run, document/chunk counts, errors, embed-cache hits, and the recent run history.
  • GET /knowledge/api/knowledge/status — the same data as JSON.
  • index is optional; when given, the page also shows the backend type and count().

It requires the web extra (pip install "reactifact[web]") and is mounted independently from the traces router. The traces dashboard keeps describing agent runs; /knowledge describes corpus builds.

docs.title: What is intentionally absent
docs.text:
• YAML pipelines and a knowledge CLI.
  • A plugin registry / type strings.
  • Answer synthesis, reranking and chat — use reactifact.quick.rag, reactifact.providers and reactifact.recipes.
  • Evaluation and tracing — use reactifact.eval and reactifact.tracing.

Keeping those out of knowledge is what makes it a capability layer rather than a second framework inside reactifact.

docs.title: MCP
docs.text:
reactifact speaks MCP both ways: call tools from an external MCP server as ordinary Tools, or expose reactifact's own Tools (and a running Context) as an MCP server for Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or another agent to call into. Both require the mcp extra:

pip install "reactifact[mcp]"

Nothing in reactifact's core imports mcp — a bare pip install reactifact never pulls in the SDK; reactifact.mcp raises a readable ImportError with the install hint if you use it without the extra.

docs.title: Client: call remote MCP tools
docs.text:
mcp_stdio_tools/mcp_http_tools connect to an MCP server and yield its tools as a list[Tool] — the same Tool contract ToolUse/LLMAgent already take, so a remote MCP tool and a local @tool function are interchangeable:

from reactifact import Consume, create_step_group
from reactifact.mcp import mcp_stdio_tools
from reactifact.tools.use import ToolUse

async with mcp_stdio_tools(
    "npx", ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/tmp"]
) as tools:
    fs_agent = create_step_group(
        "fs",
        consumes=[Consume(Question)],
        steps=[ToolUse("Answer questions about files in /tmp.", tools)],
    )
    # tools (and fs_agent) stay callable for the life of the `async with` block

mcp_http_tools(url, headers=...) connects over streamable HTTP the same way — pass headers for a server that requires a static credential (e.g. {"Authorization": "Bearer ..."}). Both are thin wrappers over mcp.ClientSession — use mcp_tools(session) directly if you're managing the session yourself (a custom transport, …).

docs.title: OAuth (client_credentials)
docs.text:
For a server that requires OAuth rather than a static header, oauth_client_credentials builds an auth= value for mcp_http_tools using the client_credentials grant — machine-to-machine, no browser or human consent involved:

from reactifact.mcp import mcp_http_tools, oauth_client_credentials

auth = oauth_client_credentials(
    "https://mcp.example.com",
    client_id="...",
    client_secret="...",
    issuer="https://auth.example.com",  # the authorization server that issued them
)
async with mcp_http_tools("https://mcp.example.com", auth=auth) as tools:
    ...

issuer pins the token exchange to that specific authorization server's discovered metadata, so a compromised or misconfigured MCP server can't redirect the credential exchange elsewhere. Tokens are cached in memory for the life of the auth object (InMemoryTokenStorage); pass your own storage= to persist them across restarts.

This covers client_credentials only — the flow where the agent itself holds the credential. The authorization-code flow (a person granting consent through a browser redirect) needs a redirect_handler/callback_handler wired to whatever hosts the app, which is host-specific plumbing outside this library's scope; use mcp.client.auth.OAuthClientProvider directly for that.

docs.title: Server: expose reactifact as MCP
docs.text:
create_mcp_server builds an mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer from a list of Tools — hand-written Tool subclasses and @tool-decorated functions alike, since both already carry a JSON schema (Tool.schema) that becomes the MCP tool's real argument names and types, not one opaque **kwargs:

from reactifact.mcp import create_mcp_server
from reactifact.tools import tool

@tool
async def search_catalog(query: str, limit: int = 10) -> str:
    """Searches the product catalog."""
    ...

server = create_mcp_server([search_catalog], name="my-app")
await server.run_stdio_async()

A typed Pipeline is a tool as well — the MCP argument schema comes from seed_type, and the result is the latest answer_type:

server = create_mcp_server(
    [pipeline.as_tool(name="ask_knowledge", description="Ask the KB pipeline")],
    name="my-app",
)

destructive=True on a Tool becomes the MCP tool's destructiveHint annotation — the same signal Claude Desktop's own confirmation UI reads.

docs.title: Exposing a Context
docs.text:
Pass context= to also publish two read-only resources over MCP — an external client can inspect a running reactifact app's state, including provenance, the same way your own code does with context.list_artifacts()/ context.get():

server = create_mcp_server(tools, context=ctx, name="my-app")
  • context://artifacts/{artifact_type} — every artifact of one type, newest first (e.g. context://artifacts/Answer).
  • context://artifact/{artifact_id} — one artifact's current data and version.

docs.title: Mounting over HTTP
docs.text:
server.streamable_http_app() returns a Starlette app — mount it on the same FastAPI app as create_trace_router/create_chat_router:

app.mount("/mcp", server.streamable_http_app())

docs.title: Security model: no built-in authorization
docs.text:
reactifact's authorization is opt-in on RuntimeResources (Principal, PermissionPolicy, Access; see Trust & safety). The MCP bridge itself adds no per-resource or per-tool authorization. Concretely, for create_mcp_server:

  • The two context= resources (context://artifacts/..., context://artifact/...) are read-only — an MCP client can inspect any artifact in the Context you pass, with no per-artifact-type or per-field redaction.
  • Tools are not sandboxed by MCP exposure. Any Tool you hand to create_mcp_server is just as callable — and just as capable of mutating state — as it would be inside your own ToolUse/LLMAgent loop. If a tool can write to a database or call a paid API, an MCP client that can call it can do the same, exactly like a local tool-calling agent — MCP is a transport, not a permission boundary.

The host application owns access control: only pass a Context you're willing to expose read-only in full, and only pass Tools you're willing to let any connected MCP client invoke. Gate destructive tools the same way you would for a local HITLLMAgent (ToolUseHITL, §60) if a human approval step is needed before a mutating tool actually runs.

docs.title: Errors: ToolOutput.error → MCP is_error
docs.text: A Tool that returns ToolOutput(error=...) (or raises) surfaces to the MCP caller as is_error=True with your message intact — reactifact raises the SDK's own ToolError internally for this, the one exception type the SDK does not mask down to a generic "Error executing tool …" for the caller.

docs.title: Migrating from LangGraph / CrewAI / LlamaIndex / plain Python
docs.text:
You don't move everything at once. The recommended path is port one piece, keep it running next to the old code, and grow from there — reactifact is a library, it composes with whatever already works. This page is the how; the port matrix is the what maps to what, and each pattern below links to a runnable example.

If you only take one idea away:

State is primary, execution is derived. Instead of drawing what runs next, you declare what artifacts exist and what each agent consumes/produces; the runtime decides what runs from the state changes.

docs.title: 0. Already on reactifact?
docs.text: This page is for porting other frameworks. If you are upgrading reactifact itself from 0.1.x, use the dedicated 0.1.x → 0.20.0 migration guide.

docs.title: 1. Concept map
docs.text: You have (LangGraph / LangChain / CrewAI / LlamaIndex) reactifact node + add_edge / add_conditional_edges a Step + a Consume(Type) — the edge is "who consumes this type" a shared TypedDict/dict state, mutated by nodes typed, versioned Artifacts in the Context reducer (Annotated[list, add]) effects.create/update/link(...) compiled into one atomic Patch checkpointer / thread state Context (git-like), Session/SessionStore, context.branch()/merge() interrupt() / Command(resume=...) human.ask(...) → PendingQuestion, answered with human.resume(...) subgraph / nested agent AgentAsTool (isolated nested runtime) or context.branch() conditional router / supervisor Consume.condition / Consume.by_field, or recipes.Router RAG chain (retriever → prompt → LLM) Source + fan_out_sources + materialize_doc + produces (quick.rag for the simple case) tool loop (create_react_agent) LLMAgent/ToolUse (or ToolUseHITL for approvals), or reactifact.tools.native / recipes.run_tool_loop MemorySaver + summary node Msg artifacts + context.view + recipes.WindowSummarizer/RollingDigestSummarizer callbacks / LangSmith / Langfuse native traces (reactifact.tracing) + redactor=, export to Langfuse/OTLP/Postgres

docs.title: 2. Port one node (before → after)
docs.text:
A LangGraph node that classifies then answers:

def classify(state):            # node
    return {"route": "billing" if "invoice" in state["text"] else "general"}

def answer(state):              # node
    return {"reply": llm(state["text"], route=state["route"])}

graph.add_edge(START, "classify")
graph.add_edge("classify", "answer")

On reactifact the edges disappear — they become consumes/produces:

from pydantic import BaseModel
from reactifact import StepCall, step


class Question(BaseModel):
    text: str


class Route(BaseModel):
    thread_id: str
    kind: str


class Reply(BaseModel):
    text: str


@step(produces=Route, consumes=Question)
async def classify(call: StepCall) -> None:
    question = call.trigger
    kind = "billing" if "invoice" in question.data.text.lower() else "general"
    call.effects.create(Route(thread_id=question.id, kind=kind), id=f"route:{question.id}")


@step(produces=Reply, consumes=Route)
async def answer(call: StepCall) -> None:
    route = call.trigger  # this step runs because a Route was created
    # ... call the model with run-scoped input ...
    call.effects.create(Reply(text="…"), id=f"reply:{route.data.thread_id}")

from reactifact import Context, Runtime, create_step_group

classifier = create_step_group("classifier", steps=[classify])
answerer = create_step_group("answerer", steps=[answer])

Two things to notice, because they're the migration's real work:

  • Eligibility is a state decision, not a placement. The old graph said "answer runs after classify". Here answer runs because a Route exists — so a guard (return None when the input isn't ready) is the sequencing mechanism, not an edge.
  • Stable ids. f"route:{question.id}" makes re-runs idempotent (§42) — the same event twice never duplicates state. This replaces most hand-written "already done?" bookkeeping.

docs.title: 3. State dict → artifacts
docs.text:
# before: one growing dict
state["facts"].append({"text": "...", "source": url})

# after: typed artifacts + provenance
fact = effects.create(Fact(text="...", source=url))
fact.link("extracted_from", doc)

Nothing is mutated in place: an update is a new version, so context.diff(v1, v2) is a real operation and provenance (supported_by/derived_from/…) is the same graph the runtime uses to decide what to re-run — not a logger bolted on. See reactifact.recipes.changed_fields / downstream_fields for the recompute argument made concrete.

docs.title: 4. Checkpointing, threads, time-travel
docs.text:
• Persist conversations with SessionStore(FileKVBackend(...)) + Chat (examples/knowledge).
  • Fork an exploration with context.branch(), run different agents on each fork, and merge() them back — with a real MergeConflict when both forks touch the same artifact (examples/forklab).
  • Reproduce a past state with reactifact.replay / replay_context; pin a run's fingerprint with reactifact.audit.context_hash (examples/fintech_audit).

docs.title: 5. Interrupts → human-in-the-loop
docs.text:
# ask
human.ask("Approve the refund?", kind="approve", id=f"approve:{qid}")
# resume (from your HTTP handler / CLI)
context.resume(question.id, "yes")

The human is just another reaction (PendingQuestion is an artifact); tools can be gated the same way — see ToolUseHITL (a @tool(destructive=True) that only runs after an approval) and examples/devops.

docs.title: 6. RAG chain → sources
docs.text:
from reactifact.quick import rag

r = rag({"docs": "./docs", "costs": "./costs.csv"})
answer = await r.ask("what's the total gpu cost?")   # answer.text, answer.sources

For full control, compose the same pipeline by hand with fan_out_sources + materialize_doc and produce an Answer linked supported_by the documents (examples/knowledge). Retrieval is a Source capability (filesystem/CSV/web, or KnowledgePipeline + IndexSource for vector search), not a hardcoded chain — swap the source, keep the agents.

docs.title: 7. Tool loops
docs.text:
• Model decides which tool, one step at a time: LLMAgent / HITLLMAgent (examples/devops).
  • OpenAI-native tools/tool_calls: reactifact.tools.native (composable functions), or recipes.run_tool_loop for a bounded, parallel, mandatory-tool-aware loop.
  • Budgets and honest failure come for free: Budget(max_runs=…, max_tool_calls=…), and a produce returns None instead of a confident guess (§59).

docs.title: 8. Don't go all-or-nothing (interop)
docs.text:
• Call reactifact from a node. Your LangGraph node can build a Context, run a Runtime, and return the result — move one auditable/calculating step at a time.
  • Expose reactifact as MCP. create_mcp_server(tools, context=ctx) publishes your Tools (and read-only context://artifacts/... resources) so any MCP client — Claude, another agent framework — can call the reactifact part.
  • Coexist by concern. Keep your orchestration where it works; use reactifact where provenance, determinism, and auditability matter most (the fintech_audit shape).

docs.title: 9. Ops mapping
docs.text: Concern reactifact tracing Tracer(store=TraceStore(...)), LangfuseTracer, OTLPTracer, PostgresStore; scrub with RuntimeResources(redactor=…) sessions SessionStore over FileKVBackend/SQLiteKVBackend/PostgreSQLKVBackend budgets / limits Budget(max_runs, max_seconds, max_iterations, max_tool_calls) error policy fail-loud by default; Runtime(isolate_errors=True, on_agent_error=…) opts into partial progress per-request data Runtime.arun(request={...}) → call.request (no ContextVar plumbing) resource lifecycle RuntimeResources.scope(factory) / async with (loop-safe clients)

docs.title: 10. Migration checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Every intermediate value is a typed Artifact, not a dict/TypedDict.
  • [ ] Each unit is a Step that declares consumes/produces; no node calls another directly.
  • [ ] Eligibility is a guard (return None), not a scheduling order.
  • [ ] Ids are stable and re-derivable (f"answer:{qid}", effects.create_once(...), effects.create_once_from(...)).
  • [ ] Derived artifacts link(...) to their inputs (provenance).
