  • [ ] Model calls go through structured_llm/llm_reply and return None on failure — the caller shows an honest fallback, never a fake answer.
  • [ ] A Budget is set for production runs.
  • [ ] Human steps are human.ask/resume, not a special case.
  • [ ] Sessions use SessionStore; resources are built per loop (RuntimeResources.scope).
  • [ ] Tracing is wired (Tracer(store=...)), and redactor= is set if data is sensitive.

docs.title: 11. Gotchas
docs.text:
• There is no add_edge. If you find yourself wanting one, the edge is a Consume(ProducedType) on the downstream agent.
  • effects, not return patch. Write effects.* and return None; the runtime compiles the effect set into one atomic commit (Step returning a Patch is the low-level escape hatch, not the idiom).
  • Artifacts aren't messages. Model input is built from a context.view(...) / consumed artifacts, not a free-floating string list.
  • Determinism is a habit. Use stable ids and keep timestamps/randomness out of what you hash — context_hash then makes runs comparable (examples/fintech_audit).

docs.title: 12. Where to look next
docs.text:
• Port matrix — canonical pattern → reactifact example.
  • Quickstart — the four quick cases in a few lines.
  • Scheduler semantics — the execution contract you're moving onto.
  • Patterns / Recipes — reusable building blocks.

docs.title: Migrating from reactifact 0.1.x to 0.20.0
docs.text:
This guide is for applications that already use reactifact. If you are porting from LangGraph, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, or plain Python, start with Migrating from other frameworks instead.

0.20.0 is a breaking release, but the migration is mechanical for most apps: the runtime and the commit DAG are the same, while the authoring surface gains explicit types. The old names remain importable through the 0.20 compatibility window; this page shows the replacements and what to plan for 0.23.0.

0.24 removed the old agent names

Agent, create_agent, validate_agents, the agents= keyword and the reactifact.agents module are gone. Read every Agent below as StepGroup (create_agent as create_step_group, agents= as groups=).

docs.title: 1. What changed
docs.text:
0.1.x 0.20.0 Produce / @produce / ProduceCall Step / @step / StepCall StepGroup.produces=[...] StepGroup.steps=[...] contracts split between StepGroup.consumes and Produce.reacts_to each step owns consumes / produces call.trigger + manual isinstance guards typed T / Artifact[T] inputs, or Consume(T) manual context.get(stage_id(...)) scope= / Scope(...) + typed inputs, or Latest[T] self.effects.* effects: Effects in a class run(), or call.effects in a function step mutable Artifact with artifact.update() frozen handle; updates go through Context / Effects artifact.history / .at() / .diff() Context.version_history / artifact_version / version diffs v1 session payload v2 blobs + data_ref; v1 payloads migrate on load reactifact.tool_use, reactifact.native_tool_use, reactifact.agent_tool reactifact.tools.use, reactifact.tools.native, reactifact.tools.agent

Everything marked as a bridge remains importable in 0.21.x, but the top-level Produce/ProduceCall/@produce are no longer in __all__. Produce/ProduceCall/@produce are removed in 0.23.0; the old Agent names are removed in 0.24.0, and the remaining bridges stay through 0.24.x. The tool-module shims were removed in 0.25.0; old persisted type ids still resolve, but new imports use the canonical paths in the table above.

docs.title: 2. Steps and agents
docs.text:
The class form keeps the same shape — declarations move onto the step and the body receives typed inputs:

from reactifact import Artifact, Effects, Produce, Step


class Estimate(Produce):
    artifact_type = Project
    reacts_to = Project

    async def produce(self, call: ProduceCall) -> None:
        self.effects.update(call.trigger, stage="estimate")

becomes:

from reactifact import Artifact, Effects, Step


class Estimate(Step):
    consumes = (Project,)
    produces = (Project,)

    async def run(self, project: Artifact[Project], effects: Effects) -> None:
        effects.update(project, stage="estimate")

The agent lists steps instead of produces:

group = StepGroup(produces=[Estimate()])

becomes:

group = StepGroup(steps=[Estimate()])

StepGroup.produces remains a compatibility property. New code should use StepGroup.steps; read group.steps when introspecting a group.

The function form changes @produce to @step, and call.effects replaces self.effects:

from reactifact import step


# Answer and Evidence are your own models.
@step(produces=Answer, consumes=Evidence)
async def answer(call):
    return Answer(text=call.trigger.data.text)

Function steps may also take typed inputs:

@step(produces=Answer, consumes=Evidence)
async def answer(evidence: Evidence, effects: Effects) -> Answer:
    return Answer(text=evidence.text)

docs.title: 3. Typed inputs and correlation
docs.text:
In 0.1.x a step opened with guards:

if call.event is None or not isinstance(call.trigger.data, Question):
    return None
question = call.trigger.data

In 0.20.0 the input contract is the type annotation:

class Research(Step):
    consumes = (Question,)
    produces = (Answer,)

    async def run(self, question: Question, effects: Effects) -> Answer:
        return Answer(text=question.text)

Use Artifact[T] instead of T when the step needs the handle, id, or provenance. Use list[Artifact[T]] for every matching version of a type.

Correlation that used to be a stable-id lookup is now a Scope:

class BuildAnswer(Step):
    consumes = (
        Consume(ResearchTurn),
        Consume(Evidence, wakes=False),
    )
    produces = (Answer,)
    scope = "query_id"

    async def run(
        self,
        turn: ResearchTurn,
        evidences: list[Artifact[Evidence]],
        effects: Effects,
    ) -> None:
        ...

scope= keeps artifacts with the same query_id together. Consume(..., wakes=False) is the replacement for reading an input without re-running on every update. Latest[T] selects the newest value when a step should not see the whole history. Use When(...) for value conditions and Wakes(False) for non-waking inputs.

docs.title: 4. Effects
docs.text:
self.effects is gone. A class step receives effects: Effects; a function step uses call.effects:

0.1.x 0.20.0 self.effects.create(value) effects.create(value) self.effects.update(artifact, **fields) effects.update(artifact, **fields) self.effects.link(source, "relation", target) effects.link(source, "relation", target) self.effects.announce(...) effects.announce(...)

Returning a BaseModel from run() is create-sugar. Anything beyond creating the declared output — updates, links, extra creates, HITL — goes through effects. The declarations still validate the commit: every created type must be listed in produces; put the primary output first, then any extra creates: produces=(Receipt, PendingAction) (the old also_creates= spelling was a deprecated alias).

docs.title: 5. Artifacts and version history
docs.text:
Artifact is now a frozen handle into a content-addressed version store. Do not mutate it and do not call artifact.update().

0.1.x 0.20.0 artifact.update(data) ctx.update(artifact.id, data) (returns a new handle) artifact.history ctx.version_history(artifact.id) artifact.at(version) ctx.artifact_version(artifact.id, version) artifact.diff(other) ctx.version_diff(...) / ctx.diff(...)

The old Artifact.at/history/diff methods remain as deprecated bridges in 0.20.x. Compaction is authoritative: ctx.compact(keep_versions=...) selects which versions remain readable, and deleted artifacts keep readable history. Code that relied on a mutable _history list should read versions through Context.

docs.title: 6. Sessions and persistence
docs.text:
Session payloads are v2: an artifact version index plus blobs keyed by (data_type, content_hash), with commit Create/Update operations using data_ref.

No code change is needed for existing stores: Context.from_dict still loads v1 payloads, and the next save writes v2. If you inspect payloads directly, read versions through the public Context methods rather than depending on the old data/history layout.

docs.title: 7. Tool imports
docs.text:
The old top-level modules are shims. Prefer the package paths:

from reactifact.tools import tool
from reactifact.tools.use import ToolUse, ToolUseHITL
from reactifact.tools.native import parse_tool_calls
from reactifact.tools.agent import AgentAsTool
0.1.x 0.20.0 reactifact.tool_use reactifact.tools.use reactifact.native_tool_use reactifact.tools.native reactifact.agent_tool reactifact.tools.agent

The shims stay importable through the 0.21 compatibility window and are kept through 0.24.0.

docs.title: 8. Removed examples
docs.text: The 0.1.x tree contained many small examples that duplicated the same idea. 0.20.0 keeps ten reference applications: devops, knowledge, forklab, repair, medic_lab, fintech_audit, starter_app, chat, outbox, and repo_agent; tour isolates the primitives. If an old example was your starting point, use the closest survivor and the patterns page. The deleted examples are not part of the public API.

docs.title: 9. Migration checklist
docs.text:
1. Replace Produce with Step, ProduceCall with StepCall, and @produce with @step.
  2. Replace StepGroup(produces=[...]) with StepGroup(steps=[...]); move StepGroup.consumes contracts onto the relevant steps.
  3. Replace self.effects.* with the injected effects argument, or call.effects in function steps.
  4. Replace call.trigger.data guards with typed parameters, Consume(...), Latest[...], or When(...).
  5. Replace manual stable-id correlation with scope= / Scope(...).
  6. Replace artifact.update() with ctx.update(); move history reads to Context.version_history / artifact_version.
  7. Update tool imports to reactifact.tools.*.
  8. Search for leftovers:
rg "self\.effects|Agent\(produces=|\.update\(.*artifact|artifact\.history|reactifact\.tool_use|reactifact\.native_tool_use|reactifact\.agent_tool" .
  1. Run the test suite and fix DeprecationWarnings for @produce and the history bridges. Tests should pass without warnings from your own code.
  2. If you persist sessions outside SessionStore, verify a stored v1 payload still loads and is rewritten as v2 on save.

docs.title: 10. Compatibility and removal
docs.text:
Removed in 0.23.0:

  • Produce, ProduceCall, @produce

Removed in 0.24.0:

  • Agent, create_agent, validate_agents, agents=, reactifact.agents

Kept as deprecated bridges through 0.24.x:

  • StepGroup.produces
  • Artifact.at, Artifact.history, Artifact.diff

Removed in 0.25.0:

  • reactifact.tool_use, reactifact.native_tool_use, reactifact.agent_tool

@produce emits a DeprecationWarning; the aliases and bridges do not. Treat all of them as migration aids, not as a second API.

If something in your app has no direct mapping, check the 0.20.0 changelog and the patterns page before opening an issue.

docs.title: Migrating to reactifact 0.23.0
docs.text:
This guide is for applications that already use reactifact. It covers the new facade and authoring surface added in 0.23.0; the runtime, artifacts and provenance model are unchanged.

The short version:

0.22 style 0.23 style ChatAssistant(..., user_message=Q, agents=[...]) Chat(..., seed_type=Q, groups=[...]) create_message + a category ContextVar seed_factory(text, session_id, request) stream() override around the turn per_turn(text, session_id, request) context manager Runtime(ctx, agents=[...]) Runtime(ctx, groups=[...]) or steps=[...] tool collaborator via closures/globals Annotated[Client, Inject()] (+ Depends alias) tool returns a string to parse tool returns a pydantic model / list[Model] Tracer(store=...) manually Pipeline(traces=...), Chat(traces=...) recipe subclasses Recipe.from_funcs(...).pipeline(...)

ChatAssistant is still available as the low-level engine behind Chat; it is no longer the recommended entry point.

docs.title: 1. Chat: ChatAssistant → Chat
docs.text:
Before:

assistant = ChatAssistant(
    store=store,
    groups=[echo_group],
    user_message=UserMsg,
    reply=reply,
    session_state=session_state,
    resources=lambda: build_resources(),
)

After:

chat = Chat(
    store=store,
    groups=[echo_group],
    seed_type=UserMsg,
    answer_type=Reply,
    reply=reply,
    session_state=session_state,
    resources=lambda: build_resources(),
)
  • seed_type= replaces user_message=;
  • answer_type= lets chat.answer() return the typed artifact;
  • invoke/stream/history keep working;
  • chat.router() is the FastAPI router, chat.test_client() the isolated in-memory client;
  • chat.traces=/trace_sample=/lifespan= mirror Pipeline.

docs.title: Category, tenant or user per turn
docs.text:
Before, apps often used a create_message hook and a ContextVar. After, take the value from request in seed_factory:

def seed(text: str, session_id: str, request: Mapping[str, object]) -> UserQuery:
    return UserQuery(
        text=text,
        session_id=session_id,
        category=str(request.get("category") or ""),
    )

chat = Chat(..., seed_type=UserQuery, seed_factory=seed)
await chat.invoke("...", session_id="s1", request={"category": "helm"})

create_message is still accepted for HITL/resume flows; seed_factory is the short path for normal turns. For turn-scoped contextvars (a vault, a knowledge namespace), use per_turn, an async context manager:

@asynccontextmanager
async def per_turn(text, session_id, request):
    token = set_current_vault(SecretVault(...))
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        reset_current_vault(token)

chat = Chat(..., per_turn=per_turn)

quick.chat_agent(...) now returns Chat; it accepts groups=/steps=. The deprecated agents= alias was removed in 0.24.

docs.title: 2. Groups, steps and aliases
docs.text:
Runtime(ctx, agents=[...]) was a deprecated alias, removed in 0.24. Use the keyword that describes what you pass:

Runtime(ctx, groups=[MyGroup()])     # StepGroup instances
Runtime(ctx, steps=[MyStep()])       # raw steps, wrapped in implicit groups

Agent/create_agent/validate_agents and agents= were removed in 0.24; use StepGroup/create_step_group/validate_contracts(groups=...) and groups=/steps=.

docs.title: 3. Tools: injection, typed results, policies
docs.text:
A plain-class parameter is injected from RuntimeResources and omitted from the JSON schema:

@tool
async def get_pod(name: str, k8s: K8sClient) -> Pod:
    return Pod(name=await k8s.get(name))

When the type would be ambiguous (a dataclass, a protocol, a scalar-looking service), mark it explicitly:

from typing import Annotated
from reactifact import Inject

@tool
async def get_pod(name: str, k8s: Annotated[K8sClient, Inject()]) -> Pod:
    ...

Depends is a FastAPI-style alias for Inject. Both forms are supported:

  • Annotated[T, Inject()] — preferred;
  • param: T = Inject() — shorthand.

Other 0.23 tool changes:

  • a pydantic return fills ToolOutput.data; a non-empty list[Model] becomes {"items": [...]} instead of str(list);
  • @tool(retry=RetryPolicy(...), timeout=...) retries exceptions and ToolError(retryable=True), and bounds one attempt;
  • ToolUse reports ToolError.code/retryable to the model;
  • outside a step, pass resources explicitly: execute_tool(tool, args, resources=... ).

docs.title: 4. Recipes: from subclasses to functions
docs.text:
PlanExecute and ReflectionLoop can still be subclassed, but the function form is shorter and builds the group/pipeline for you:

flow = PlanExecute.from_funcs(
    goal_type=Goal,
    step_type=PlanStep,
    result_type=StepResult,
    final_type=FinalAnswer,
    plan=plan,
    execute_step=execute_step,
    finish=finish,
)
pipeline = flow.pipeline(seed_type=Goal)

ReflectionLoop.from_funcs(...) follows the same shape. flow.group() returns a StepGroup for an existing Runtime.

docs.title: 5. Tracing: sampling and retention
docs.text:
The manual Tracer(store=...) wiring is no longer required:

pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[...], traces=True, trace_sample=SamplingPolicy(rate=0.1))
chat = Chat(steps=[...], seed_type=Q, traces="traces.db")

Old traces can be pruned from the CLI:

reactifact traces prune traces.db --keep 5000 --days 30 --dry-run
reactifact traces prune traces.db --keep 5000 --days 30 --keep-failed --keep-tag incident

See observability for RetentionPolicy and sampling.

docs.title: 6. Pipeline parity
docs.text:
• Pipeline.answer(seed) / await Pipeline.aanswer(seed) return the typed answer_type, like Chat.answer().
  • Pipeline(trace_sample=...) is honoured by TestPipeline as well; TestPipeline.answer()/aanswer() delegate.
  • TestChat.override(Type, instance) replaces a typed resource in the test client.

docs.title: 7. Compatibility and removals
docs.text:
• Produce / ProduceCall / @produce are removed; use Step/@step/ StepCall.
  • also_creates= / reacts_to= on steps are removed (deprecated since 0.20); declare outputs in produces=(Primary, Extra) and inputs/triggers in consumes=(...) (or Consume(..., wakes=False)).
  • Effects.ask / Effects.resume / Effects.act are removed; inject Human/Outbox instead (human.ask/resume, outbox.act). These three had no separate deprecation release: 0.23 is the first release with their replacements, so this is a deliberate exception to the one-minor window.
  • Agent, create_agent, validate_agents, agents= and the reactifact.agents module are removed in 0.24.0.
  • ChatAssistant, StepGroup.produces, Artifact.at/history/diff remain deprecated bridges through the 0.24.x line. New code should use Chat, StepGroup, StepGroup.steps and Context.version_history/artifact_version/version_diff.
  • The tool-module shims (reactifact.tool_use, reactifact.native_tool_use, reactifact.agent_tool) were removed in 0.25.0; use reactifact.tools.use/.native/.agent. Old persisted type ids that still name the removed modules (e.g. reactifact.tool_use.ToolAnswer) resolve through reactifact.types.resolve.

docs.title: 8. Migration checklist
docs.text:
1. Replace ChatAssistant(..., user_message=..., agents=...) with Chat(..., seed_type=..., groups=...).
  2. Move per-turn metadata into seed_factory/request; move contextvars into per_turn.
  3. Replace Runtime(..., agents=[...]) with groups=/steps=.
  4. Mark ambiguous tool collaborators with Inject() and return pydantic models/lists.
  5. Replace recipe subclasses with from_funcs(...) where the function form fits.
  6. Switch trace wiring to traces=/trace_sample= and add a retention policy.
  7. Replace effects.ask/act/resume with the injected Human/Outbox, and move also_creates=/reacts_to= into produces=/consumes=.
  8. Run the test suite and search for the old spellings:
rg "ChatAssistant|agents=|user_message=|reactifact\.tool_use|@produce|also_creates|reacts_to|effects\.(ask|act|resume)"

docs.title: Migrating to reactifact 0.24.0
docs.text: 0.24 adds a lot, but it also finishes the hard breaks planned for this line: the old agents names are gone, core LLM helpers take a provider instead of a context, and the optional knowledge layer tightens its contracts. There is no compatibility shim for the items below.

docs.title: The 0.x agents names are removed
docs.text:
Agent, create_agent, validate_agents, the agents= keyword and the reactifact.agents module are gone. Runtime.agents is now Runtime.groups.

Before:

from reactifact import Agent, Runtime, create_agent

group = create_agent("qa", steps=[answer])
runtime = Runtime(context, agents=[group])

After:

from reactifact import Runtime, create_step_group

group = create_step_group("qa", steps=[answer])
runtime = Runtime(context, groups=[group])

The same keyword change applies to ChatAssistant, run_subflow, swarm and quick.chat_agent. validate_agents(...) becomes validate_contracts(groups=...).

docs.title: Artifact[T] | None now means "handle or None"
docs.text: An optional artifact parameter used to fall through to the data path and return the model. It now returns the Artifact[T] handle (or None). Use T | None when you want optional data; Artifact[T] and list[Artifact[T]] still return handles.

docs.title: Optional provider parameters resolve from resources
docs.text: A step parameter typed LLMProvider | None (and other optional services) now receives the registered provider instead of silently staying None. If None was your "no provider, use a fallback" signal, check resources.has(...) or make the parameter required.

docs.title: Pending HITL replies are waiting: true
docs.text: When a PendingQuestion exists, Chat returns a structured question payload with waiting: true instead of an ordinary reply. Branch on waiting rather than assuming every reply has reply; Chat(resume_pending=True) turns the next user message into the answer.

docs.title: LLM helpers
docs.text:
Before:

from reactifact.structured import structured_llm

body = await structured_llm(context, schema=Answer, user=text)

After — use the injected provider (the usual case inside a step):

@step(consumes=Question)
async def answer(question: Question, llm: LLMProvider) -> Answer:
    return await llm.structured(Answer, user=question.text)

Or pass the run's provider explicitly when you only have a Context:

body = await structured_llm(context.resources.llm, schema=Answer, user=text)

The same change applies to:

  • json_schema_llm / llm.structured_json(...);
  • llm_reply / llm.reply(...);
  • chat_complete / chat_complete_full / llm.chat(...);
  • StructuredLLM.call(llm, user).

llm may be None; the helpers keep their honest None / on_error("no_provider") fallback. The old context= keyword is removed — pass the provider directly (a clear TypeError is better than silently accepting a Context in a provider slot).

docs.title: Knowledge point IDs include the chunk index
docs.text:
point_id(source_uri, text) now also hashes the chunker's chunk_index when it is present. Two identical section bodies in one document no longer collapse into a single point.

Effect: every existing knowledge index gets new point IDs. Run one full (non-incremental) reindex after upgrading — pipeline.run() without incremental=True, or clear the index first. This is a storage migration, not a schema change; no data is lost.

docs.title: DocStore is a protocol
docs.text:
DocStore now names the backend contract; instantiate JsonDocStore (the default) or SqliteDocStore:

from reactifact.knowledge import JsonDocStore, SqliteDocStore

json_store = JsonDocStore(".reactifact/knowledge/state.json")
sqlite_store = SqliteDocStore(".reactifact/knowledge/state.sqlite3")

pipeline.run(state_path=...) still uses JsonDocStore; pass docstore= to choose SQLite. Both expose the same entry/commit/save/record_run/ runs/snapshot surface.

docs.title: MemoryIndex.count is async
docs.text: index.count (property) is now await index.count(), matching SqliteIndex, QdrantIndex, PgVectorIndex and ChromaIndex. The status router checks the CountableIndex protocol.

docs.title: Hybrid retrieval fails loudly
docs.text:
Two silent degradations became ConfigError:

  • min_score with hybrid=True — RRF scores are ranks, not similarities;
  • hybrid=True on an index without keyword_search — use hybrid=False (ChromaIndex is dense-only).

docs.title: Hit diagnostics and SourceRef.fragment
docs.text: SearchHit gained dense_rank, keyword_rank, rerank_rank, score_kind and chunk_id (all additive). SourceRef gained fragment; knowledge refs use the chunk id as their fragment, so chunks of one document now get distinct artifact ids. Stored refs without a fragment keep their old ids (fragment defaults to "").

docs.title: consume() removed
docs.text: The lowercase consume(...) factory duplicated Consume(...) and is gone. Use Consume(Type, ...) or a lifecycle subclass (OnCreate, OnUpdate, OnDelete, OnStale) directly. It had no separate deprecation release; 0.24 is a deliberate exception to the one-minor window.

docs.title: Additive highlights
docs.text:
• Lifecycle consume classes: OnCreate, OnUpdate, OnDelete, OnStale.
  • Progress collaborator for UI statuses without Context.
  • Owned resources (RuntimeResources.register(..., owned=True)).
  • Pydantic resources and implicit read-only inputs.
  • Optional artifact handles and the Ensure primitive.
  • SqliteDocStore, vector-dimension validation and runtime-checkable index capabilities.
  • HttpConnector/S3Connector, CSV/JSON/PDF/DOCX extractors and batched ingestion.
  • MMR diversity, section/document expansion and retrieval metrics.

docs.title: Migrating to reactifact 0.25.0
docs.text: 0.25 is mostly additive ergonomics. Two planned removals are the only breaking changes; if you do not use EmbeddingSource or the old tool-module shims, no code changes are needed.

docs.title: EmbeddingSource is removed
docs.text:
The core no longer ships a vector Source. Build retrieval with the optional knowledge layer and expose it through IndexSource.

Before:

from reactifact.sources import EmbeddingSource

source = EmbeddingSource("./docs", embedder=embedder)

After:

from reactifact.knowledge import (
    FilesystemConnector,
    IndexSource,
    KnowledgePipeline,
)

pipeline = KnowledgePipeline(
    FilesystemConnector("./docs", source_id="docs"),
    embedder=embedder,
    index=index,
)
source = IndexSource(pipeline, hybrid=True)

IndexSource keeps the regular Source contract (asearch/resolve) and adds hybrid search, MMR diversity, reranking and ACL filtering. To keep a bespoke vector store, implement Source.asearch yourself; FileSystemSource, CSVSource and WebSource remain in the core.

This removal had no separate deprecation release: 0.25 is a deliberate exception to the one-minor window, because the knowledge layer now covers the case end to end.

docs.title: Tool-module shims are removed
docs.text:
reactifact.tool_use, reactifact.native_tool_use and reactifact.agent_tool completed their 0.20–0.24 compatibility window and are gone. Use the canonical modules:

Removed Use reactifact.tool_use reactifact.tools.use reactifact.native_tool_use reactifact.tools.native reactifact.agent_tool reactifact.tools.agent

Persisted type ids that still name a removed module resolve through reactifact.types.resolve, so stored sessions keep loading.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Every run records a trace. Traces are observable by default: the demo dashboards work offline with no external services, and you can additionally ship traces to Langfuse or Postgres.

docs.title: What a trace contains
docs.text:
A RunTrace is one run of the runtime (until astream/run ends):

  • Agent spans (AgentSpan) — what each agent did: artifact reads and writes, the key/value summary of the patch it produced, the consumed artifact type that triggered it (event_artifact_type), which produces actually ran (produces: name, authored operations, latency), and which tools it executed (tools: ToolRun name/produce/latency/status/chars/output — args are opt-in, output is truncated/redacted by the trace policy). The dashboard, OTLP (reactifact.tracing) and Langfuse (langfuse.observation.metadata.tools) carry the same list; Langfuse/OTLP also emit a child span per tool, placed by ToolRun.started_at (parallel calls overlap). Tool args are omitted by default — set RuntimeResources(record_tool_args=True) to include them (scrubbed by redactor=). Tool.execute is instrumented on the class, so a direct call inside a step lands in the same tools list as execute_tool.
  • Agent contract (AgentContract) — the declared consumes/produces/ tools/priority, plus the concrete event_artifact_id. The Work view renders explicit consumes → produces lists, mutes declared-but-not-run items, and a click on any chip filters the visible spans.
  • LLM calls (LLMCall) — prompts, responses (truncated), token usage, latency, and the step that made the call (LLMCall.step), so the waterfall nests it under that step.
  • Timing and ordering — the whole causal chain of a run, in order. Agent spans, steps (StepRun.started_at), LLM calls (LLMCall.started_at) and tools (ToolRun.started_at) carry wall-clock starts, so the timeline can place parallel work and nested calls without guessing.

A huge run is read in pages: get(span_limit=…, span_offset=…) (default 500) returns span_total/has_more_spans, the detail UI loads more on demand, and Mermaid is built only for a capped window. Write-time caps (Tracer(limits=TraceLimits(...))) mark a trace trace_truncated instead of letting it grow without bound. DELETE /api/traces/{id} and DELETE /api/sessions/{id} (or delete_run/delete_session) remove a bad run or session; the session itself stays visible until you choose to delete it.

RecordingLLM wraps your provider for free, so LLM call tracking needs no code — just wire it at resources time.

docs.title: SQLite store + web dashboard (local, offline)
docs.text:
from reactifact.tracing import TraceStore

store = TraceStore("traces.db")   # SQLite sink; also serves runs back to the UI

The store's interface is async (export/query/get); the SQLite core runs in a worker thread, so the same object works in a web app and in plain sync code.

The dashboard is a FastAPI router mounted on your app:

from reactifact.tracing.web import create_trace_router

app.include_router(create_trace_router(store), prefix="/traces")

It serves a small app shell (shared templates/app.css): a collapsible sidebar (Traces / Sessions), /traces (list of runs, filterable), /traces/{id} (stat tiles, spans, reads, writes, LLM input/output, timing, a native causal chain (runtime → agent → step → LLM/tool → commit) and a live Mermaid evidence graph — written artifacts with patch.link provenance edges, §34), and /sessions. The devops example mounts this router and is the reference UI.

Opening a run starts with the overview — wall time, work, spans, LLM/tool time, errors and tokens:

The Work card has two views. Tree groups spans by agent and shows the declared Consume → Step contract plus what actually ran; no-op steps are dimmed, and clicking a chip filters the visible spans:

Waterfall puts span → step → LLM/tool on one time axis, so parallel work and the latency bottleneck are visible at a glance:

Branches appears when the run has a parent or children: it links to the parent run and lists child runs (branch, outcome, duration) fetched from /api/traces/{id}/children. The list API also accepts branch= and parent_run_id= filters, and child ordering is oldest-first — no client-side tree building needed.

Causal chain is the readable "why did this happen" view: Runtime → agent on the triggering artifact, then each step with its LLM/tool calls, then the commit. Click an event to focus and outline its span in Tree/Waterfall:

docs.title: Portable reports (no FastAPI)
docs.text:
A trace is not tied to the dashboard. RunTrace renders itself:

trace = await store.get(run_id)
print(trace.to_text())        # terminal
print(trace.to_markdown())    # PR comment / CI summary
print(trace.to_html())        # one self-contained file

The CLI mirrors this and can compare two runs:

reactifact trace traces.db <run_id> --format text
reactifact trace traces.db <run_id> --format html --out trace.html
reactifact trace traces.db <run_id> --against <other_id>

Pipeline(traces=True) or traces="traces.db" records every run without building a Tracer by hand; result.trace_id and await result.trace() read it back. This is the non-FastAPI path: scripts, notebooks and CI use the same trace store.

docs.title: Retention (disk and audit)
docs.text:
RetentionPolicy controls what the store deletes:

from reactifact.tracing import RetentionPolicy

store = TraceStore(
    "traces.db",
    retention=RetentionPolicy(
        max_runs=5000,            # newest unprotected runs
        max_age_days=30,          # TTL, even inside max_runs
        keep_failed=True,         # never delete failed/stopped
        keep_tags=frozenset({"incident", "bad-prompt"}),
    ),
)

The policy runs after every export (and on demand). The CLI is the ops path:

reactifact traces prune traces.db --keep 5000 --days 30 --dry-run
reactifact traces prune traces.db --keep 5000 --days 30 --keep-failed --keep-tag incident

Protected runs (failed, tagged) do not count against max_runs; they can make the store larger, by design.

docs.title: Sampling (production volume)
docs.text:
Tracer(sample=...) applies tail sampling before any sink sees the run:

from reactifact.tracing import SamplingPolicy, Tracer

tracer = Tracer(
    store=store,
    sample=SamplingPolicy(
        rate=0.01,                       # 1% of successful runs
        always_on_error=True,            # keep all failed/stopped runs
        always_if=lambda t: t.duration_ms > 3000,
    ),
)

Sampling is deterministic by run id, so a given run is consistently in or out of the sample. Use rate=1.0 for dev/test and a low rate plus always_on_error in production.

docs.title: Reviewing runs: tags and notes
docs.text:
The dashboard is also the review surface. After inspecting a trace you mark the run with a tag (bad-prompt, hallucination, needs-review, …) and an optional note describing what is wrong / what to change. Tags live in the store, not in the runtime — they are annotations attached to a run_id after the fact, so the immutable trace the runtime produced is never rewritten.

  • The list page shows tag facets with counts (click to filter), tag chips per run, free-text search (run / session / agent / error), sortable columns (click a header), token and latency rollups, a live toggle and a JSON export of the current filter. Every filter/tag/sort/page lives in the URL, so a view is a shareable link; name one and it is kept as a saved view.
  • A sessions page (/sessions) groups runs by session_id with run count, total duration, tokens and last-seen, and links into the filtered trace list.
  • The run page has a Review card: add/remove tags, each with a note.
  • Tree ↔ Waterfall: the run's work is shown either grouped by agent, or as a hierarchical Gantt waterfall (span → step → LLM/tool) with start offset and width by latency, making parallelism and the latency bottleneck obvious. Clicking a causal-chain event jumps to and outlines its span in the active Tree/Waterfall view.
  • In-trace search filters spans/agents/LLM text; copy link, copy JSON and a raw JSON view are one click away.
  • Select several runs to tag or untag them in bulk.
  • manage tags renames, recolours or deletes a tag across every run.
GET    /api/traces?tag=bad-prompt&tag=review&tag_mode=all&q=refund&sort=duration_ms
GET    /api/tags                       # facets: name, colour, count
POST   /api/traces/{id}/tags           # {tag, note}
DELETE /api/traces/{id}/tags/{tag}
POST   /api/traces/tags                # bulk: {run_ids, tag, note}
POST   /api/traces/tags/remove         # bulk: {run_ids, tag}
PATCH  /api/tags/{name}                # {new_name, color}
DELETE /api/tags/{name}
GET    /api/traces/export              # full traces for the current filter
GET    /api/sessions                   # runs grouped by session, with rollups

Both backends implement the same annotation API: SQLite keeps tags/run_tags tables (created and migrated automatically), Postgres mirrors them as TEXT/TIMESTAMPTZ with cascading deletes. Point create_trace_router at either and the review workflow behaves identically.

docs.title: Configurable columns from artifacts
docs.text:
Give the traces table columns pulled from the run's artifacts — e.g. the user's question and the final answer:

from reactifact.tracing import TraceColumn

app.include_router(create_trace_router(
    store,
    columns=[
        TraceColumn(label="Question", agent="route", type=UserMsg,
                    field="text", direction="read"),
        TraceColumn(label="Answer", type=ChatReply, field="text"),
    ],
))

A TraceColumn names the column and where its value comes from: which agent's span, which artifact type (a class or its name), direction (read / write / any), and a dotted field into the artifact's data. A list step takes its first element unless an explicit index is given, so sources.title means sources[0].title and sources.1.title the second. Several matches: index defaults to the last. A missing artifact, a — default, or JSON cut off by the trace size limit all fall back to default.

scope="session" resolves a column as of the row's run: it looks at every run up to and including that one, in chronological order, instead of just the row's run. The read order is reversed, so the triggering artifact (recorded first) is treated as the most recent and the default index=-1 means "latest so far". A chat is many turns, and a HITL clarify splits one exchange into two runs (the ask turn, then the resume turn) — so Question = the message that started the current exchange (index=-1), shown on the resume row too, and Answer = the latest reply so far (— until it exists).

Columns are computed server-side per run and returned in each /api/traces item as fields (GET /api/columns lists the labels). The dashboard renders them in the list (with a column chooser, visibility persisted per browser) and, on the run page, as a Fields card — so the question/answer (and a HITL clarify, e.g. a PendingQuestion column) are visible on the run too, not just the list. Values come from the JSON persisted with each span, clipped by TraceLimits(max_data_chars=…) on the tracer (preferred) or the legacy RuntimeResources(trace_truncate=…) (default 1500 chars; None disables the clip) — raise it if a deep/large field must resolve.

The devops and repair examples wire this up (Question + Answer, and the latter also Stage + a pending HITL Pending).

docs.title: Langfuse and Postgres as additional sinks
docs.text:
A trace can go to several places at once via CompositeTracer, passed to the Runtime. Tracers are thin: on_turn_begin → on_span → on_turn_end (only on_turn_end performs I/O; sinks export asynchronously).

from reactifact import Runtime
from reactifact.tracing import LangfuseTracer, PostgresStore, TraceStore

runtime = Runtime(
    ctx,
    groups=[...],
    tracer=[
        TraceStore("traces.db"),                        # local dashboard
        LangfuseTracer(public_key="...", private_key="...",
                       host="https://cloud.langfuse.com"),
        PostgresStore(dsn="postgresql://…"),            # pg extra required
    ],
)

Spans are delivered once per turn end (delivery-once semantics); the Langfuse tracer maps read/write summaries into input/output, so the timeline is readable in their UI; each step run the agent performed also becomes a child observation, so the waterfall shows the Consume → Step steps. The SQLite TraceStore stays a source for the web dashboard; Postgres mirrors the same runs/spans schema.

Both TraceStore and PostgresStore implement TraceReader (async query/get), so create_trace_router works against either: point the dashboard at PostgresStore(dsn) to view traces written to Postgres without a local SQLite file.

docs.title: OTLPTracer: any OTLP/HTTP collector
docs.text:
LangfuseTracer is Langfuse-specific (its own langfuse.* attribute namespace). OTLPTracer exports the same run as vendor-neutral spans — GenAI semantic-convention attributes only (gen_ai.*, plus a reactifact.* namespace for reads/writes/provenance) — to any OTLP/HTTP collector: Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog Agent, a local otel-collector, ...

from reactifact.tracing import OTLPTracer

runtime = Runtime(
    ctx,
    groups=[...],
    tracer=OTLPTracer(endpoint="http://localhost:4318/v1/traces"),
)

No opentelemetry-sdk dependency — like LangfuseTracer, it POSTs the OTLP/HTTP JSON payload directly over httpx (already a core dependency), so this needs no extra to install. Pass headers= for a collector that requires auth.

LangSmith ingests OTLP and maps the gen_ai.* conventions:

OTLPTracer(
    endpoint="https://api.smith.langchain.com/otel/v1/traces",
    headers={
        "x-api-key": os.environ["LANGSMITH_API_KEY"],
        "Langsmith-Project": "my-project",   # optional (default: "default")
    },
)

Self-hosted LangSmith uses https://<your-host>/api/v1/otel/v1/traces with the same headers.

SigNoz takes OTLP/HTTP directly — no key self-hosted:

# self-hosted
OTLPTracer(endpoint="http://<signoz-host>:4318/v1/traces")
# SigNoz Cloud
OTLPTracer(
    endpoint="https://ingest.<region>.signoz.cloud:443/v1/traces",
    headers={"signoz-ingestion-key": os.environ["SIGNOZ_INGESTION_KEY"]},
)

The same works for Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog and a local otel-collector. To fan out to several back ends at once — or to redact before export at the collector — point endpoint at an OpenTelemetry Collector and let it route; RuntimeResources.redactor already strips trace text before it leaves the process (see Redacting sensitive data).

docs.title: Metrics (Prometheus)
docs.text:
Traces answer "what happened in this run"; metrics answer "how are runs doing overall" — the numbers you alert on. reactifact.metrics has no dependency beyond the core: an in-process collector plus a Tracer that fills it, and a /metrics router.

from reactifact.metrics import Metrics, MetricsTracer, create_metrics_router

metrics = Metrics()
runtime = Runtime(ctx, groups=GROUPS, tracer=MetricsTracer(metrics))
app.include_router(create_metrics_router(metrics))   # GET /metrics

It records, per finished turn: reactifact_runs_total{outcome}, reactifact_budget_exceeded_total{outcome}, reactifact_agent_runs_total{ agent,status}, reactifact_agent_latency_seconds{agent}, reactifact_llm_calls_total{provider,model,agent}, reactifact_llm_tokens_total{kind,provider,model}, reactifact_llm_errors_total{provider,model}, reactifact_tool_calls_total{tool,status}, reactifact_tool_errors_total{tool}, reactifact_tool_latency_seconds{tool}, and — with MetricsTracer(metrics, pricer=…) — reactifact_llm_cost_total{provider,model}.

Straight from the span's reads/writes/edges you also get domain-adjacent counters with no app code — reactifact_artifacts_written_total{type,op}, reactifact_artifacts_read_total{type}, reactifact_relations_total{relation} — so whatever artifact types and relations the app uses (e.g. an Answer/Evidence pair and supported_by) show up automatically.

For app-specific signals (a route, a refusal, a source), record them from a produce through RuntimeResources.metrics — a no-op sink until configured, so there is no None to check:

metrics = Metrics()
runtime = Runtime(
    Context(resources=RuntimeResources(metrics=metrics)),
    groups=GROUPS,
    tracer=MetricsTracer(metrics),
)

# inside a step, at the decision point:
call.context.resources.metrics.increment("route_total", route=route)
call.context.resources.metrics.observe("docs_found", len(docs), source=source)

Metrics.render() emits the Prometheus text exposition directly (no prometheus_client), so create_metrics_router just serves it; MetricsTracer also composes with the sinks (tracer=[TraceStore(…), MetricsTracer(metrics)]). As with traces, only state-changing agents emit spans, so a settle-only generation isn't counted.

docs.title: Emission model
docs.text:
• Only state-changing agents emit spans (a pure read/verify step emits nothing — less noise).
  • One Tracer per CompositeTracer: hand the same composite to multiple sinks.
  • on_turn_end is the single delivery point: a new astream/arun advances the run id (a re-run counts as a new run), and each turn's trace is finalized once.

docs.title: Live lifecycle hooks
docs.text:
A finished RunTrace is the source of truth, but a UI often needs to show work while it happens. Tracer exposes optional, sync, best-effort hooks:

class LiveTracer(Tracer):
    def on_agent_start(self, agent, event, reads): ...
    def on_agent_retry(self, agent, attempt, error): ...
    def on_tool_start(self, tool, args): ...   # args is redacted or None
    def on_tool_end(self, run): ...             # ToolRun
    def on_commit(self, commit): ...            # after the patch is applied

They are called alongside the existing on_turn_begin/on_span/on_turn_end. Keep them non-blocking (enqueue to a bounded queue; do the I/O elsewhere): an exception in a hook is logged and swallowed, so observability can never fail the run.

docs.title: Streaming LLM calls
docs.text: RecordingLLM records complete() and stream() calls. A streamed call is recorded once, after the stream ends (or is closed), with the concatenated text, terminal token usage and any error; the stored response is clipped to trace_truncate (default 1500). The per-chunk overhead is one async-generator frame, no per-token recording.

docs.title: Typed run events (astream_events)
docs.text:
Runtime.astream() is the legacy status stream (ProgressEvent: run start, status text, run end). For a live UI/Studio, use astream_events, which yields typed RunEvents and selects what you need:

async for event in runtime.astream_events(
    stream_mode=["debug", "updates", "values", "messages"]
):
    match event:
        case AgentStart(agent=name): ...
        case ArtifactWrite(writes=writes): ...
        case LLMDelta(delta=text): ...
        case RunEnd(outcome=outcome): ...
mode events custom CustomEvent — Context.announce(...) updates ArtifactWrite after each committed patch values Values — context diff after each commit debug GenerationStart, AgentStart, AgentRetry, AgentEnd, ToolStart, ToolEnd messages LLMDelta chunks (streamed, or one final delta for complete())

RunStart, RunEnd and RunFailed are always emitted; a failed run yields RunFailed and then re-raises the original exception. Events are best-effort: the internal queue is bounded and drops the oldest item rather than back-pressuring the runtime.

docs.title: Workspace scope and metadata
docs.text:
A shared trace store can serve several workspaces. Stamp runs either on the runtime or per request:

Runtime(..., trace_scope="workspace-42")
# or, per turn:
await runtime.arun(request={
    "workspace_id": "workspace-42",
    "trace_metadata": {"user_id": "u1", "agent_version": "v3"},
})

RunTrace.scope and RunTrace.metadata are stored with the run; store.query(scope="workspace-42") and store.sessions(scope=...) filter by it (also exposed as ?scope= on the dashboard API). trace_scope wins over request["workspace_id"].

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
reactifact writes structured, correlated logs under the reactifact.* logger namespace and stays silent until you turn it on (a library never configures the root logger):

import sys

from reactifact import configure_logging

configure_logging()               # INFO, human-readable, to stderr
configure_logging(json=True)      # one JSON object per line
configure_logging(level="DEBUG", stream=sys.stderr)

Every line carries the turn's correlation fields — run_id, session_id, generation, agent, and the request_id from runtime.arun(request=…) — so a line ties back to the exact run/agent. Add your own with bind(...):

from reactifact import bind, get_logger

log = get_logger(__name__)

with bind(tenant="acme", user="bob"):
    log.info("handling request")

Levels: run started / run finished and action dispatched are INFO; per-generation and per-agent completion are DEBUG, and a failing agent or a failed dispatch is WARNING. Logs are metadata — artifact data and prompt contents are never logged. Logging complements tracing: a RunTrace is the durable audit of a run; these logs are what an operator tails while it happens.

docs.title: Tracing never fails the run
docs.text: Observability is best-effort by contract. A sink that is unreachable (Langfuse down, Postgres refusing connections), a custom Tracer callback that raises, or a malformed trace payload is caught, logged as a warning, and skipped — the business run completes normally and the next turn is traced as usual. When several sinks or tracers are configured, a failing one never prevents the others from receiving the trace. Losing observability should never mean losing the run it was only supposed to observe.

docs.title: Redacting sensitive data
docs.text:
Traces leave the process (SQLite, Postgres, Langfuse, a dashboard, a log line); the working Context — and, when a session is saved, the resumable conversation — does not. Set redactor= on RuntimeResources to scrub the text that leaves: artifact data, LLM messages/response, and span/LLM error. The live state and persisted sessions are deliberately not redacted — masking the working copy would corrupt a conversation that is supposed to resume.

from reactifact import RuntimeResources
from reactifact.redaction import RegexRedactor

resources = RuntimeResources(llm=from_env(), redactor=RegexRedactor())

The built-in RegexRedactor is conservative on purpose — email, US SSN, IBAN, Bearer tokens and sk-…-style API keys — so it never masks a legitimate financial figure; pass patterns=[(name, regex), …] for a project's own formats (cards, phones, …). Any object with a redact(text: str) -> str method satisfies the hook, so a PII service drops in without subclassing. None (the default) leaves traces byte-for-byte as before.

Tool observations are not trace text — they go back into the model's prompt. If tools can return secrets, pass redact_tool_outputs=True to recipes.run_tool_loop: it applies the same resources.redactor before the observation is fed to the LLM and recorded on ToolLoopResult.observations.

docs.title: Progress events (UI reactivity)
docs.text:
For the animated "Думаю… / Составляю план… / Считаю смету…" lines, inject progress: Progress into a step and call it:

async def run(self, question: Artifact[Question], progress: Progress) -> Evidence:
    progress("Ищу в документации…")
    ...

Progress is a thin view over Context.announce(message, kind=..., **payload): both publish ProgressEvents on the EventHub, which the runtime yields to the SSE stream. Context.announce stays available for code that already holds a Context (servers, dispatchers, recipes); a step that only needs to announce should take Progress instead of the whole Context.

async for event in runtime.astream():
    if event.kind == "status":
        yield sse("status", {"message": event.message})

announce is not a log — it is a first-class UI channel that the web demos consume verbatim.

docs.title: Patterns
docs.text: Reusable patterns observed across the examples. They are not abstract — each is concretely instantiated in examples/.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
Do Don't Why Write effects.create/update/delete/link/upsert(...), return None Assemble a Patch by hand in an ordinary step The runtime compiles one atomic patch per step — building it yourself is the escape hatch, not the default Guard eligibility with an early return None Rely on scheduling order to skip work that isn't ready Eligibility is a state decision, not a lucky accident (§69) Use stable ids (answer:{qid}) or effects.create_once(...) Re-derive an id from a counter or timestamp Idempotent re-runs — the same event twice must not duplicate state Return None on missing model / failed parse, then show an honest fallback Substitute a canned "confident-sounding" answer when the LLM call fails Deterministic work stays deterministic; generative failure must be visible, not papered over Keep next_status/scoring functions pure (state) -> ... Mix LLM calls or side effects into a StatusMachine.next_status Pure functions are unit-testable without a runtime Use Runtime(isolate_errors=True, on_agent_error=...) only when you've decided partial progress is acceptable Reach for isolate_errors as a default to silence exceptions Default is fail-loud (§69) — isolating errors is an explicit product decision, not a safety net Record an outbound side effect with outbox.act(...), do the I/O in Runtime(dispatcher=...) Send an email / call a webhook directly inside run() The intent is committed state — replay, retries and merges cannot re-send it (§42)

Each row links to the fuller pattern below.

docs.title: HITL: humans as first-class participants
docs.text:
A human is just another reaction to the context. The runtime represents a question with PendingQuestion:

class PendingQuestion(BaseModel):
    question: str
    kind: str = "general"          # e.g. "clarify", "approval"
    notes: dict[str, Any] = {}     # routing info ("which agent asked")
    resolution_schema: dict | None = None   # optional JSON Schema for a form

A step creates one with human.ask(...), and the human's answer comes back through human.resume(...) (an effect that marks the PendingQuestion answered, §60):

human.ask("Approve the estimate?", kind="approval")
# ... the web/UI sees a pending question and shows a waiting state ...
human.resume(question_artifact, "да")
return None

When the UI needs a typed answer, pass a Pydantic model as schema= and resume with a model or a mapping — resolution_data carries the JSON-safe value, while resolution keeps the legacy string form:

class RefundApproval(BaseModel):
    approved: bool
    note: str = ""

human.ask("Approve the refund?", kind="approve", schema=RefundApproval)
# ...
human.resume(question_artifact, RefundApproval(approved=True, note="ok"))
# or: human.resume(question_artifact, {"approved": True})

Read it back with question.data.approved() / question.data.answer_text() (fallback to resolution keeps old code working).

The producing agent sees the answer as a new event (the corresponding PendingQuestion artifact is updated). Web demos query context.pending_questions() to know whether to render a "waiting" state.

Pattern: activate stage → immediately ask (the repair ApprovalStage creates the approval PendingQuestion the moment it becomes eligible, without waiting for a user message), then react to the answer on the next event.

For a re-derivable question (f"steer:{qid}:{round}", medic-lab's steering ask), pass id= to human.ask(...) so a guard (if context.get(id) is not None: return None) can stop the step from asking again while the question is still unanswered — the same idempotency idiom as effects.create_once.

docs.title: Outbox: external side effects
docs.text:
A step should never perform external I/O itself — send an email, call a webhook, deploy. It records the intent and the runtime performs it, once, after the intent is committed:

from reactifact import Artifact, Effects, Outbox, PendingAction, Runtime, Step


class Notify(Step):
    consumes = (Order,)
    produces = (Receipt, PendingAction)  # outbox.act creates a PendingAction

    async def run(
        self, order: Artifact[Order], effects: Effects, outbox: Outbox
    ) -> None:
        # stable, content-derived key -> idempotent re-runs and merges
        outbox.act(
            "notify",
            key=f"notify:{order.data.id}:email",
            payload={"to": order.data.email, "order": order.data.id},
        )
        effects.create(Receipt(order_id=order.data.id), id=f"receipt:{order.data.id}")


async def dispatch(context: Context, action: Artifact[PendingAction]) -> None:
    if action.data.kind == "notify":
        await send_email(action.data.payload, idempotency_key=action.data.idempotency_key)


runtime = Runtime(ctx, groups=[Notify()], dispatcher=dispatch)

The runtime dispatches every committed-but-undispatched PendingAction after a generation commits (and keeps the turn alive until the outbox is empty), marking each dispatched — or failed (then re-raising) if the dispatcher throws. A failing dispatcher must be idempotent on action.data.idempotency_key, because resume is at-least-once (durability).

Why it holds up:

  • Replay reconstructs state without running the runtime, so it never re-sends; the replay CLI reports dispatched / pending / failed counts.
  • Retries re-derive the same id, so outbox.act returns None — no second intent. Two produces in one generation (snapshot isolation) both see nothing, but the outbox dedupes at drain.
  • Branches that independently reach the same action share the id and merge to one intent; a dispatched side wins whichever branch is the merge target, so a merge never re-sends an already-sent action. Divergent payloads under one id raise MergeConflict.
  • Merge is pure state: it never dispatches. Call await runtime.flush_pending_actions() after a merge if no new trigger will run.
  • Operations: there is no background relay — the next arun() drains the outbox, and flush_pending_actions() drains it without a generation (call it on startup and periodically from your own timer). A failing dispatcher marks the action failed (bumping attempts), fires Runtime(on_dispatch_error=...), and re-raises; retry_action(id) re-arms it. Backoff/retry policy belongs to the application or the dispatcher.

docs.title: Tool agents: LLM + tools (blocking or HITL)
docs.text:
For "the model decides which tool to call" flows, use the built-in agents:

from reactifact import Consume
from reactifact.llm_agent import HITLLMAgent

class OpsAgent(HITLLMAgent):
    name = "ops"
    system = "You run Kubernetes/GitLab/Ansible tasks."
    tools = [...]        # FunctionTool instances
    max_steps = 8
    max_asks = 2
    consumes = [Consume(Project)]
    steps = [BuildReport()]  # your step: consumes ToolAnswer -> Report
  • LLMAgent — blocking loop: the LLM emits tool_call, the runtime runs the tool, the observation feeds the next step. No human in the loop.
  • HITLLMAgent — same, plus the LLM can emit ask: a PendingQuestion is created, the loop pauses, and the human's answer returns as Observation(source="user"). Tool execution itself is also gated by ToolUseHITL, so risky commands wait for a human click before running.

The devops example is the canonical HITLLMAgent demo (LLM tool router + approval for K8s/GitLab/Ansible mutations).

docs.title: Deferred tool groups: many tools without the context cost
docs.text:
Connecting several MCP servers (or any large tool sets) means every one of their schemas would otherwise land in the system prompt on every step, most of them never called. DeferredToolGroup keeps a group's tools out of the prompt — only its name, description, and bare tool names show up in a compact catalog — until the LLM asks for it by calling the built-in load_tools tool. ToolUse/LLMAgent support it; ToolUseHITL/ HITLLMAgent don't yet (see the class docstring for why):

from reactifact.tools.use import DeferredToolGroup, ToolUse
from reactifact.mcp import mcp_stdio_tools

async def load_github_tools():
    async with mcp_stdio_tools("npx", ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"]) as tools:
        return tools

github_group = DeferredToolGroup(
    group_id="mcp:github",
    display_name="GitHub",
    description="Issues, PRs, repos, code search",
    tool_names=["create_issue", "search_repos", "create_pr"],
    loader=load_github_tools,
)

ToolUse(
    system="...",
    tools=[...],                       # always-visible tools
    deferred_tool_groups=[github_group],  # hidden until requested
)

loader runs at most once per group per ToolUse run — the group's real tools (full schemas) join the regular tool list for the rest of that run once loaded.

docs.title: Structured output: never parse raw JSON yourself
docs.text:
The runtime wraps a single LLM call into a pydantic schema with retries and lenient JSON parsing:

The first argument is an LLMProvider — usually an injected llm: LLMProvider; code with only a Context can pass context.resources.llm. Functions and provider methods share the same parse/retry policy.

from reactifact.structured import StructuredLLM, structured_llm

# procedural variant:
body = await structured_llm(
    llm, schema=AnswerBody,
    system="You assemble coherent answers.",
    user=f"Question: {question}\nFacts: {facts}",
)

# re-usable object variant:
_extractor = StructuredLLM(ProjectInfo, system="Extract repair facts; unknown = null")
facts = await _extractor.call(llm, user=message_text)

Both return None on a missing model or a parse failure after retries — and the caller is expected to handle None (see fallbacks). If you need to tell "no provider configured" apart from "the provider is down" (e.g. to alert on a real outage) without changing that None handling, pass on_error:

def alert_if_down(reason: str, exc: Exception | None) -> None:
    if reason == "provider_error":
        logger.error("LLM outage: %r", exc)

body = await structured_llm(llm, schema=AnswerBody, user=text, on_error=alert_if_down)

Build the system/user strings with PromptTemplate (core): declared variables, a KeyError on missing vars, and model-attribute fields (template.render(topic=…, question=…)) — no hand-rolled .format in app code. For a reusable pair use PromptPair(SYSTEM, USER).render(...), whose .as_kwargs() also passes the prompt hash.

StructuredGenerateAgent is the declarative wrapper: override build_prompt(inputs), optionally fallback(inputs), declare schema — and the reading/writing provenance is recorded for you.

docs.title: Plan-and-execute: draft once, run one step at a time
docs.text:
For a goal that decomposes into an ordered sequence of dependent steps, use the PlanExecute recipe. The recipe owns ordering, gating, idempotent re-entry and completion; your domain supplies three hooks:

class Flow(PlanExecute[Goal, PlanStep, StepResult, FinalAnswer]):
    goal_type = Goal
    step_type = PlanStep
    result_type = StepResult
    final_type = FinalAnswer

    async def plan(self, context, goal): ...
    async def execute_step(self, context, step, history): ...
    async def finish(self, context, goal, results): ...


class FlowAgent(StepGroup):
    steps = Flow().produces()

PlanExecute runs exactly one step per generation and re-triggers itself from the new StepResult; the last result triggers finish. See tests/test_recipe_plan_execute.py for the runnable cases.

docs.title: Correlating across artifact types
docs.text:
Consume.condition only ever sees the single artifact matched by its own type — it can't look at a different type's instance to decide whether to fire. The real cases that need that ("a Report and its answered PendingQuestion exist for the same thread", "no HelpdeskTicket has been filed for this thread yet") used to get hand-rolled inside run(), exactly the guard logic consumes exists to keep out of there. reactifact.consume.CorrelatedConsume (and its two single-purpose factories) puts that back where it belongs — on the class declaration:

from reactifact.consume import AbsentConsume, JoinConsume

class ApprovalGate(StepGroup):
    consumes = [
        JoinConsume(
            Report, PendingQuestion,
            key=lambda d: d.thread_id,
            part_conditions={PendingQuestion: lambda d: d.answered},
        ),
    ]
    steps = [RecordApproval()]

class TicketGate(StepGroup):
    consumes = [
        AbsentConsume(Report, absent_type=HelpdeskTicket, key=lambda d: d.thread_id),
    ]
    steps = [FileTicket()]

JoinConsume(*parts, key=...) fires once every listed type exists for the same key; AbsentConsume(type, absent_type=..., key=...) fires for type only where no matching absent_type exists yet for the same key. Both are thin factories over CorrelatedConsume(require=..., forbid=...) — reach for CorrelatedConsume directly when a case needs both at once (required present and forbidden absent), which neither factory alone can express without nesting one inside the other. the step reads inputs the same way it would read a mixed list from several ordinary Consumes — no isinstance/scan guard needed inside the body.

docs.title: Selecting one of several triggers
docs.text:
Each step owns its consume contract, so an agent with several steps does not need a global trigger: a step that consumes ResolvedDocuments simply does not run for a DecisionReply event.

class FinalizeWithDocuments(Step):
    consumes = (ResolvedDocuments,)
    produces = (DraftAnswer,)

    async def run(self, docs: Artifact[ResolvedDocuments]) -> DraftAnswer:
        return DraftAnswer(query_id=docs.data.query_id, source="documents")


class DirectFinalize(Step):
    consumes = (DecisionReply,)
    produces = (DraftAnswer,)

    async def run(self, reply: Artifact[DecisionReply]) -> DraftAnswer:
        return DraftAnswer(query_id=reply.data.query_id, source="direct")

For conditional selectors, use Consume.by_field/by_status or Annotated[T, When(...)] on the step. The runtime skips the step entirely for events outside its contract, so the body needs no type guard. A DELETED event on the step's own consumed type is the one exception: trigger is None there (the data is gone); use call.event/event: Event when reacting to deletions.

docs.title: Reacting to deletions
docs.text:
Consume listens to CREATED/UPDATED by default. A step that must react when an artifact disappears includes the event type explicitly:

from reactifact import Artifact, Consume, Context, Effects, Event, EventType, Step

class ResetPlan(Step):
    consumes = (
        Consume(PlanStep, event_types=(EventType.ARTIFACT_DELETED,)),
    )
    produces = (Project,)

    async def run(
        self,
        context: Context,
        event: Event,
        effects: Effects,
    ) -> None:
        assert context.get(event.artifact_id) is None
        project = context.latest(Project)
        if project is not None:
            effects.update(project, plan=[], stage="plan")

Two rules for deletion-reactive steps:

  • There is no trigger artifact — the data is gone. Take event: Event (or call.event), not Artifact[T]; use event.artifact_id / event.artifact_type.
  • The version store keeps history: ctx.get(id) is None, while ctx.version_history(id) / find_versions(...) still return prior versions.

Caveat: today Context.delete() emits only ARTIFACT_DELETED and does not mark dependents STALE (unlike update()). If deleting an input should invalidate derived artifacts, either handle it in an explicit deletion-reactive step or mark those dependents stale yourself. Treat this as the deletion contract until the core grows delete→stale invalidation.

docs.title: Reading input without waking up on it
docs.text:
An explicit consumes is the wake set; the typed run() signature is the read set. A type in the signature but not in consumes is collected as a read-only input — "read this, don't wake up on it." The recurring case: an agent that should run when a Question arrives but also wants ConversationHistory as input, without re-running once per history artifact:

consumes = (Question,)

async def run(self, question: Question, history: ConversationHistory) -> ...:
    ...

history is collected, validated and recorded as an input, but never wakes the step. Consume(..., wakes=False) remains for an explicit consumes list with no typed param; when consumes is derived from the signature, Annotated[T, Wakes(False)] marks one read-only input. triggers= is still the right tool for the imperative style (an StepGroup subclass overriding run() directly, with no consumes at all) — there's no Consume there to attach a condition to.

docs.title: Debouncing fan-out
docs.text:
A fan-out step that creates several artifacts of one type in a single commit (five Evidence from one search step) fires one event per artifact. An agent consuming that type by default runs once per event — five times for one batch. Consume(..., debounce=True) collapses same-generation events for that Consume into a single run:

consumes = [Consume(Evidence, debounce=True)]

The single run reads inputs (collected fresh from Context), not event — that's exactly the "which one changed" information debouncing discards, so a debounced step should never key off event for anything beyond "something changed." Debouncing is scoped to the Consume it's set on, not the whole agent: an agent with a mix of debounced and non-debounced Consumes only collapses the debounced type's events. A debounced run also correctly costs one against Budget(max_runs=...), not one per collapsed event.

docs.title: Fallbacks: honest degradation
docs.text:
Deterministic work stays deterministic; generative work degrades honestly:

  1. If no model is configured — use the deterministic variant (canned options, fallback plans): demo mode without a key.
  2. If a model returns nothing usable — do NOT substitute canned answers; report the failure openly: "Не удалось подобрать варианты…".

The repair example implements both paths in _make_design_options: fallback_options only when context.resources.llm is None, otherwise a clear failure message.

docs.title: Cost/rollback model ("change → rebuild")
docs.text:
Long multi-stage conversations occasionally need to go back. The repair example models this as: parse the change request → determine the earliest stage affected → reset everything downstream deterministically:

target = rollback_target(changed)      # "plan" | "estimate" | …
updates = _downstream_resets(target)   # clears design_options/plan/estimate
updates |= {"stage": target, "info": new_info, "handled_msg": ""}

Resetting handled_msg re-arms the stages so the rebuild actually runs. This is the manual twin of StatusMachine — for those workflows where rollback is part of the product, not a lifecycle.

docs.title: Budget and fairness
docs.text:
Budget caps a run:

runtime = Runtime(ctx, groups=[...], budget=Budget(max_runs=200), max_concurrency=2)
  • max_runs, max_iterations, max_seconds, tool-call caps — the runtime stops and reports RunOutcome (completed | budget_exhausted | …) with RunStats.
  • StepGroup.concurrency_limit (LLM-bound agents default to a lower cap) + the runtime's global max_concurrency keep provider rate limits happy — the medic-lab demo runs a hypothesis laboratory with a LLM-limit of 2 inside a global cap of 6.
  • By default one agent's exception propagates out of arun()/astream() and stops the whole run (§69 — fail loud, not silently). Opt into isolating it instead with Runtime(isolate_errors=True, on_agent_error=...): that agent contributes no patch this generation, unrelated agents still make progress, and the failure is traced (AgentSpan.error) and counted (RunStats.errors) rather than hidden.

docs.title: Chat memory with sessions
docs.text:
State lives in the context, so chat memory is just state. Across requests:

store = SessionStore(FileKVBackend("sessions"))
session = await store.open(session_id, resources=resources)
# ...create UserMsg, astream, await session.save()

store.open rehydrates the context from the last checkpoint; a background step (Consume/trigger) can trim history, update a handled_msg pointer, and patch pending questions. The web demos ship this pattern verbatim.

docs.title: Status machines for long lifecycles
docs.text:
See recipes. The rule of thumb for choosing between patterns:

Situation Approach An artifact moves through phase states StatusMachine + a verification step A workflow needs to roll back on user edits stage guard + _downstream_resets Explore & compare alternative states branch() + merge() (§39-§40) "Which of these did the model pick?" PickStage-style parse + guard

docs.title: Determinism as a habit
docs.text:
• The step contract: write effects.create/update/delete/link/upsert(...) and return None; the runtime compiles the slot into one atomic patch (§24). Patch is the transport — you rarely type it in an ordinary step.
  • Make eligibility a guard, not a lucky scheduling accident (return None early).
  • Prefer stable ids (answer:{qid}, ref:{sid}:{owner}) → idempotent re-runs. effects.create_once(Model(...), id=...) folds the "already done" guard into the call — None back means skip, don't rebuild the guard by hand above every create.
  • Pure decision functions (next_status) are unit-testable without a runtime.
  • Every LLM call has a structured schema, a retry budget, and a None path.

docs.title: Port matrix — canonical agent patterns on reactifact
docs.text:
Which classic example from LangGraph / LangChain / CrewAI / AutoGen / Haystack / DSPy we express, and how. Each row maps a canonical idea to our idiom and to a concrete example (examples/).

Canonical idea Showed by Our idiom Example ReAct tools loop LangGraph, LangChain LLMAgent/HITLLMAgent + ToolUse/ToolUseHITL, FunctionTool devops HITL tool approval (interrupt/gate) LangGraph, CrewAI human.ask → human.resume (§60) devops, repo_agent Time-travel / checkpoint branching LangGraph Context.branch(), parallel runtimes, three-way merge() forklab RAG (retrieve→augment→generate) LangChain, Haystack, LlamaIndex sources + fan_out_sources + materialize_doc + evidence→claims knowledge Structured output / extraction / router LangChain StructuredLLM / PromptTemplate / llm_reply everywhere Staged pipeline w/ replanning (a stage-driven state machine) LangGraph Project.stage-guarded steps + changed_fields/earliest_stage/downstream_fields (change→rebuild) repair Evaluation-driven dev (DSPy) DSPy reactifact.eval multi-level metrics (§56) tests + kept examples Tool budget / honesty on failure — Budget + deterministic fallbacks, None paths (§59) devops, repair External side effects (outbox) — outbox.act + Runtime(dispatcher=...), stable id, replay-safe state outbox Code review / diff analysis — deterministic rule steps + optional StructuredLLM findings, linked report code_review Framework primitives (versions, selectors, durability) — version_history/diff/compact, Latest/Wakes/debounce, SessionStore/replay tour

Everything above runs offline (deterministic fallbacks) and, with a model via .env, uses the real LLM — see docs/en/effects.md for the mental model, and docs/en/recipes.md for the building blocks.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text: Providers are capabilities — LLMs, embedders, image/speech/video models. They live in reactifact.providers, never in the core package. The app wires the ones it needs into RuntimeResources; the core communicates with them only through narrow contracts (LLMProvider, EmbeddingProvider, …).

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
The core itself knows these contracts:

Contract Role LLMProvider text generation (complete, stream) EmbeddingProvider vector embeddings ImageProvider image generation SpeechProvider / TranscriberProvider TTS / STT VideoProvider text → video generation

LLMRequest / LLMResponse / LLMResponseChunk and Message are the wire types. FakeLLM and FakeEmbedder ship in providers.fake — deterministic stand-ins so demos and tests run with no API keys.

docs.title: The env-based switchers
docs.text:
The simplest wiring is *_from_env factory functions that read .env:

from reactifact.providers import (
    embedder_from_env,
    image_from_env,
    llm_from_env,
    openrouter_llm,
)

resources = RuntimeResources(llm=llm_from_env() or openrouter_llm())
emb = embedder_from_env()
if emb is not None:
    resources.embedder = emb
img = image_from_env()
if img is not None:
    resources.set("images", img)

Pattern: llm_from_env() or <vendor default>. If no key is set the factory returns None, and the demo falls back to deterministic behavior (this is why every example keeps working with no API key at all).

from_env(**overrides) bundles the exact two-branch version of that pattern every example's local build_llm() hand-rolls (OPENROUTER_API_KEY first, else OPENAI_BASE_URL, else None), for apps that want the common default without copying that block:

from reactifact.providers import from_env

llm = from_env(max_tokens=2048)  # openrouter_llm(...) or llm_from_env(...) or None

The in-repo examples prefer the explicit factories (openai_llm(...), openrouter_llm(...)) with an explicit max_tokens — each demo defines a small build_llm() that reads .env and picks the provider, so you always see which provider runs and it stays offline-capable when no key is present.

docs.title: Declarative provider specs
docs.text:
LLMSpec is the settings-shaped alternative to a hand-written build_llm() branch. It names the provider, credentials, network knobs and fallback policy once; build() returns a provider or None and reports why:

from reactifact.providers import LLMSpec

llm = LLMSpec(
    provider="openrouter",              # or "openai", "openai-compatible"
    model="deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash",
    api_key_env="OPENROUTER_API_KEY",
    proxy="http://proxy:3128",
    temperature=0.0,
    max_tokens=2048,
).build(
    on_error=lambda reason, exc: print("llm unavailable:", reason),
)
  • provider covers every chat factory: openai, openrouter, anthropic, gemini, azure, ollama, cerebras, deepseek, fireworks, github-models, groq, mistral, nvidia, perplexity, qwen, together, xai, zai, plus openai-compatible/compatible/local/vllm/lmstudio. Aliases: claude, google, github, nvidia-nim.
  • Provider-native defaults stay in the factory: OpenRouter fast mode (reasoning disabled), Anthropic x-api-key/raw-key and 4096 tokens, Gemini x-goog-api-key, vendored OpenAI-compatible auth env vars, ollama without a key. Set auth_header/auth_scheme only to override; raw_key=True sends the key without a scheme.
  • azure maps base_url to the resource endpoint and model to the deployment; ollama builds without a key. openai-compatible requires base_url.
  • api_key is excluded from repr; api_key_env names the variable. An explicit api_key/api_key_env never silently falls back to the provider's conventional env var.
  • allow_anonymous=True covers a local endpoint with no auth (Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio). It is explicit: a missing key is a configuration outcome, not a silent unauthenticated run.
  • extra_headers/extra_body/stream_usage are passed only to providers that accept them (native Anthropic/Gemini APIs differ); the rest of the fields are common.
  • build() returns None and calls on_error("missing_key" | "missing_base_url" | "unknown_provider" | "build_error", exc); invalid constructor values still raise ValueError. The app keeps its deterministic fallback.

docs.title: Chat providers
docs.text:
OpenAICompatProvider is the generic OpenAI-compatible client and is the backing for the vendor factories. It supports:

  • api_base / custom proxy (base URL) and auth_scheme/auth_header.
  • _network_knobs — proxy/auth header/auth scheme resolved from <PREFIX>_PROXY/<PREFIX>_AUTH_HEADER/<PREFIX>_AUTH_SCHEME or explicit overrides.
  • retry_attempts (default 3) — 429/5xx and transport errors (connection reset, timeout) retry with exponential backoff; 4xx never retries. Applies to complete() only, not stream() (a stream that fails mid-way can't be retried without duplicating already-yielded chunks) — see Reliability below.
  • stream for token-wise LLMResponseChunks.

11 of the vendor *_llm factories below (Cerebras, DeepSeek, Fireworks, GitHub Models, Groq, NVIDIA NIM, Perplexity, Qwen, Together, xAI, z.ai) are generated from one _openai_compat_llm(env_prefix=..., default_model=..., default_base_url=...) factory-builder — each vendor module is a 3-line config, not a hand-copied function.

Factory Vendor openai_llm / openai_embedder OpenAI anthropic_llm Anthropic mistral_llm / mistral_embedder Mistral deepseek_llm DeepSeek openrouter_llm / openrouter_embedder / openrouter_speech OpenRouter (multi-vendor: chat, images, video, embeddings, TTS — not STT, see below) groq_llm / groq_transcriber Groq (fast inference; Whisper STT) xai_llm xAI (grok) together_llm / together_embedder Together AI fireworks_llm / fireworks_embedder Fireworks azure_llm Azure OpenAI cerebras_llm Cerebras (fast inference) github_models_llm GitHub Models qwen_llm / qwen_embedder Qwen/百炼 (DashScope) nvidia_nim_llm / nvidia_embedder NVIDIA NIM perplexity_llm Perplexity zai_llm Z.ai ollama_llm local Ollama gemini_llm Google Gemini (GeminiProvider)

Every embedder/speech/transcriber factory above is verified against that vendor's own docs, not assumed from "OpenAI-compatible chat" — some capabilities that look like they should exist don't, in an API-compatible shape. One concrete example: OpenRouter's /audio/transcriptions (STT) takes a base64-JSON body, not the multipart file upload OpenAICompatTranscriber (and every other transcriber here) expects — a real API difference, so there is deliberately no openrouter_transcriber.

docs.title: Image, speech, video
docs.text:
